    Restored to Calder’s blueprint, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    “It’s totally phenomenal,” he noted, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Recent findings suggest that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    It has been revealed that “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    In a recent development, it was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he mentioned. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and remarked he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he remarked. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”.

    In a recent development, quilici remarked he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy stated at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    It has been revealed that “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most notable and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement remarked.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    It has been revealed that “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” noted Kim Shirley.

    Industry observers note that in addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    Recent findings suggest that but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower noted.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The latest clouds, he noted, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he stated.

    Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I stated it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he noted, gazing up at it.

    Culture Is Driving Fresh Interest in Travel for Ramadan

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skift

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Longer stays and a rise in cultural visits suggest Ramadan is becoming a more significant season in Abu Dhabi’s tourism calendar.
    • This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.
    • Industry observers note that ramadan has traditionally been viewed as a quieter month for travel in the Gulf.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Longer stays and a rise in cultural visits suggest Ramadan is becoming a more significant season in Abu Dhabi’s tourism calendar. The Department of Culture and Tourism - DCT Abu Dhabi now sees an opportunity to turn the holy month into a more deliberate travel proposition for both visitors and the global travel trade.

    This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

    Industry observers note that ramadan has traditionally been viewed as a quieter month for travel in the Gulf. However, early data from DCT Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan 2026 season suggests that old assumptions about the holy month may be changing. The average length of stay across Abu Dhabi increased 3% year-on-year, while domestic hotel guests stayed 31% longer. Visits to cultural institutions more than doubled, rising from around 131,000 in Ramadan 2025 to over 291,000 in 2026.

    Skift Studio spoke with Abdulla Yousuf, director of international operations at DCT Abu Dhabi, to explore how the emirate is making Ramadan a more intentional part of the visitor experience.

    Skift Studio: How have international visitors and the travel trade traditionally viewed visiting Abu Dhabi during Ramadan, and how has that changed in recent years?

    Abdulla Yousuf: Some international travelers and travel trade partners have historically viewed Ramadan as a period when activity may be lower across the region, especially regarding opening hours, dining options, and the availability of visitor experiences. We’ve collectively worked on changing that perception over the past few years. Abu Dhabi remains open during Ramadan. Our world-class hotels, cultural landmarks, theme parks, dining venues, and beaches remain open without interruption throughout the Holy Month.

    In a recent development, what changes during Ramadan is not operational capacity, but the emirate’s rhythm. It transforms into a culturally rich season of community and reflection during the day, which gives way to an electric, festive atmosphere after sunset. The travel trade is increasingly recognizing that Ramadan is a value-added cultural window that cannot be experienced at any other time of the year.

    Recent findings suggest that abu Dhabi saw an increase in the average length of stay during Ramadan 2026. What do you take from that change, and what factors do you think may have influenced it?

    One likely contributing factor was the timing of Ramadan within Abu Dhabi’s cooler season, when comfortable temperatures make it easier to enjoy outdoor activities, such as waterfront promenades, kayaking in the mangroves, desert adventures, and visits to heritage sites.

    At the same time, Ramadan reshapes the emirate into a distinctive day-to-night journey. Calm daytime exploration of beaches, resorts, and world-class attractions transitions into evenings centered around iftars, atmospheric night markets, community suhoors, and cultural activations like Layali Nights.

    Extended opening hours make every day feel varied, immersive, and rewarding, naturally encouraging visitors to stay longer. This variety gives travel advisors and tour operators more opportunities to build itineraries that combine relaxation, culture, and outdoor experiences, helping position Abu Dhabi as a destination worth visiting during Ramadan.

    What does the 2026 data tell you about how different visitor segments are using the destination?

    The figures highlight two interesting trends. Visitors are spending longer in Abu Dhabi, and engagement with our cultural offering has increased significantly. The 31% year-on-year increase in length of stay among domestic hotel guests underscores the potential for Ramadan to drive longer stays in the domestic market. The increase in visits to our cultural institutions reinforces the importance of culture within the destination’s Ramadan offering.

    Industry observers note that the opportunity for our international travel trade partners is in communicating this diversity more effectively. Ramadan can appeal to visitors interested in culture, family experiences, hospitality, and outdoor activities, allowing partners to tailor itineraries to different traveler interests rather than treating the Holy Month as a single type of travel experience.

    What role does culture play in Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan visitor experience?

    Recent findings suggest that culture is central to the Ramadan experience in Abu Dhabi. The Holy Month offers visitors an opportunity not only to discover our cultural attractions but also to experience Emirati traditions, hospitality, and the importance of community firsthand.

    Culture during the Holy Month is lived and shared. During the day, visitors explore landmarks such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, Zayed National Museum and Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in Saadiyat Cultural District.

    It becomes deeply communal at night, from heritage games at Al Jahili Fort and Ramadan at Qasr Al Hosn to shared iftars at Ezba Experiences, and late-night visits to Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque.

    Recent findings suggest that what makes Ramadan a great time to visit Abu Dhabi? What should visitors expect?

    It has been revealed that visitors can expect a deeply authentic experience. First and foremost, Abu Dhabi is completely open for business. Every luxury resort, Michelin-recognized restaurant, shopping destination, and major attraction functions at full capacity with world-class hospitality.

    Industry observers note that after sunset, the emirate becomes remarkably vibrant. Dining evolves into a shared celebration, with iftars showcasing both global and Emirati flavors, followed by suhoors that invite people to slow down, connect, and enjoy live music, conversation, and warm hospitality late into the night. Above all, Emirati culture is rooted in generosity. International visitors are invited to sit at communal tables and build genuine connections with our community.

    With Ramadan 2027 also falling during Abu Dhabi’s cooler season (February to March), visitors can combine these cultural experiences with time outdoors, whether exploring the Corniche, enjoying our beaches or discovering the desert.

    My advice to anyone considering a visit is to embrace the distinct rhythm of the Holy Month. Ramadan offers a chance to discover Abu Dhabi at a slightly slower pace, while experiencing traditions and moments of community that make this time of year special.

    What are you hearing from tour operators and travel advisors about selling Abu Dhabi during Ramadan? Where do knowledge gaps still exist, and how does the Experience Abu Dhabi Experts Ramadan module respond to them?

    Industry observers note that some of the questions we encounter relate to practical considerations, such as opening hours, dining options, and the experiences available to visitors during the Holy Month. To address this, our International Operations team provides practical information and opportunities for first-hand experience of the destination. Our Experience Abu Dhabi Experts e-learning platform includes dedicated Ramadan training to help advisors better understand the visitor experience and communicate it to their clients.

    We complement this with international trade engagement, including workshops in 23 markets, roadshows, and familiarisation trips that allow our partners to experience Abu Dhabi and its cultural offerings for themselves.

    In a recent development, ultimately, our role is to help the travel trade move beyond general awareness of Abu Dhabi and develop a deeper understanding of the destination. The better equipped our partners are to explain what visitors can experience during Ramadan, the more confidently they can recommend it and develop relevant itineraries.

    How will DCT Abu Dhabi use learnings from Ramadan 2026 to shape the destination’s approach in 2027 and beyond?

    Industry observers note that the results from Ramadan 2026 have reinforced the importance of positioning the Holy Month as a distinctive part of Abu Dhabi’s year-round visitor offering. The increases in average length of stay and cultural engagement are encouraging and provide insights as we continue developing our approach for 2027 and beyond.

    One priority is to continue working with our tourism and hospitality partners to showcase the range of experiences available during Ramadan, from cultural attractions and outdoor activities to evening dining and community celebrations.

    Our wider ambition remains aligned with Abu Dhabi’s Tourism Strategy 2030: to attract visitors year-round, encourage longer stays, and strengthen the emirate’s position as a leading global destination. Ramadan plays an vital role in that ambition by offering international visitors a culturally distinctive, uniquely Abu Dhabi experience.

    To learn more about Abu Dhabi, visit visitabudhabi.ae.

    This content was created collaboratively by DCT Abu Dhabi and Skift Studio.

    Amadeus gained distribution share and built a bigger airline IT business. Sabre and Travelport remain weighed down by heavy debt and a heavier reliance on distribution.

    Recent findings suggest that for decades, the companies that controlled airline distribution occupied one of the most important positions in the travel industry. But making money from travel bookings and building a profitable technology business around them have turned out to be very different propositions. The contrasting fortunes of Amadeus, Sabre, and Travelport show just how different.

    It has been revealed that in 2000, Amadeus accounted for an estimated 26% of global GDS air bookings, compared with 34% for Sabre, including Abacus. Galileo and Worldspan, then separate systems that were later combined into Travelport, together had about 40%. By 2023, the estimates were 47% for Amadeus, 32% for Sabre, and 21% for Travelport, according to Redburn Atlantic data.

    Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the concern is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • It has been revealed that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the concern is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    It has been revealed that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    At matter is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly remarked it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they blueprint to bring up a vote next year.

    Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump mentioned, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    In a recent development, “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most notable stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations remarked. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the glitch.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    Photo Credit: Expedia Group agreed to acquire Czech online travel agency Kiwi.com. November 25, 2026. Grok.

    Expedia is buying its way toward becoming a one-stop shop for travel sellers and customers, even as the economics of that strategy come under pressure.

    Expedia Group agreed Wednesday to acquire Czech online travel agency Kiwi.com, expanding its European flight offering for consumers and B2B partners.

    Recent findings suggest that the companies did not disclose the price, and Expedia declined to comment on it when contacted by Skift. Kiwi generated €227 million ($264 million) in 2025 revenue.

    The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions. As Skift reported in September, Kiwi’s €100 million ($116 million) convertible bond matures June 28, 2027.

    The deal could provide an exit for majority shareholder General Atlantic, which invested in 2019. Shareholder arrangements were not disclosed.

    “Combining Kiwi.com's technology with Expedia Group’s scale will strengthen Brand Expedia and our B2B business’ position in air, giving travelers and partners more choice, confidence and value,” Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin stated in the announcement.

    In a recent development, photo Credit: Air India's new custom designed B787-9. Air India.

    IndiGo hired Air India Express' former chief as its strategy officer in March. Now Air India is creating a strategy role of its own. It looks like both airlines agree the job is worth having.

    Air India is creating a new group strategy officer position as part of its efforts to get full-service carrier Air India and its low-cost arm Air India Express working together more closely, sources remarked.

    Rival IndiGo made a similar move earlier this year, naming former Air India Express managing director and CEO Aloke Singh as its chief strategy officer. Singh ran Air India Express for five years before joining IndiGo.

    The newly introduced strategy job is one of two group-level roles being added. The other is a chief of the training academy, who will be responsible for bringing the group’s flying academy, flight training organizations and technical training under one roof.

    According to recent reports, air India CEO and managing director Tewolde Gebremariam outlined the changes at an employee town hall on Wednesday. He also spoke about operational improvements, cost cutting, network changes and the airline's longer-term intends.

    Industry observers note that ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23.

    The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under newly introduced silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

    Industry observers note that no cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1.

    U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12.

    According to recent reports, where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and said explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

    The lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

    Nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Substantial Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he indicates he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15.

    This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

    Sources indicate that neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He said chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

    In a recent development, jetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

    The parts of JetBlue’s current plan that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

    In a recent development, one caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a upcoming entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    The delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13.

    The squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

    Breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 revealed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

    Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

    Neeleman remarked Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

    Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

    Recent findings suggest that the commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

    Sources indicate that scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Big Four skip.

    Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

    Neeleman said majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

    Industry observers note that the practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman noted the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

    Sources indicate that the second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

    Reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman remarked helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

    Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the firm’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

    Sources indicate that breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has said directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13.

    Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into significant cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

    The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12.

    Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and stated chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

    Breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman intends a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its new routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

    This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

    American can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321.

    Industry observers note that scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The problem is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

    The catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 announced changes since early 2025 1.

    Sources indicate that the unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper mentioned consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45.

    Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

    — Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5.

    This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

    In a recent development, allegiant, now merged with Sun Country, serves 42 markets from Fort Lauderdale but only marginally targets former Spirit routes — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City. It is instead adding unique markets no one else flies, expanding the airport’s destination menu.

    JetBlue is Fort Lauderdale’s largest carrier and treats it as the third leg of a stool with Upcoming York and Boston, adding Mint transcons, domestic first class, and a possible lounge.

    In a recent development, the short answer: Allegiant mostly doesn’t compete with JetBlue at FLL head-to-head. It competes around it.

    Industry observers note that after Spirit shut down in May 2026, JetBlue, Frontier, Breeze, and Allegiant all added capacity at Fort Lauderdale 1. JetBlue went after Spirit’s routes directly, launching 11 newly introduced Fort Lauderdale routes on Spirit’s shutdown weekend plus a status match for Free Spirit members 3. Allegiant took a different line: of its 42 Fort Lauderdale markets, only five — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City — were Spirit cities, and it is chasing unique markets instead 1.

    That reflects the two models. Allegiant flies low-frequency leisure routes from smaller cities where it is often the only nonstop, so it avoids the daily-frequency, loyalty-driven markets JetBlue serves. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale is built around Northeast traffic, Caribbean and Latin connections — more than 20 routes to Latin America — and premium: Mint lie-flat on transcons to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, with management calling the city “Florida’s biggest premium market” 1. JetBlue is also adding its BlueFirst domestic first class and weighing a Fort Lauderdale lounge 4.

    According to recent reports, fort Lauderdale seats excluding Spirit were scheduled up a combined 40% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2026. If demand doesn’t absorb that, the thin unique routes Allegiant favors are the easiest to cut — and JetBlue, which is funding startup losses on upcoming routes while chasing a turnaround, has the most capital at risk.

    This question was addressed to Sara Nelson, International President, Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO.

    Industry observers note that customer experience and labor-as-cost coexist only when the service promise matches the cost model. The carriers now cutting hardest — KLM, Icelandair, Alaska — are protecting margin under a fuel shock, not reinventing service. The real test is where the cuts land: outsourced ground and contact-center work, and regional crews paid about half mainline, is where the customer actually meets the airline. 326.

    Recent findings suggest that the fuel shock is forcing the trade-off into the open. Jet fuel was up 102% year over year in mid-September, and record revenue has not covered it 4. American grew revenue 19.3% in Q3 and still posted a 1% operating margin because costs grew 19.7%; Delta and United each slipped about two points 6. Carriers that already settled major contracts — United’s five-year flight attendant deal carries a 31% pay increase and $741 million in retroactive pay — are paying for premium service with loyalty and premium-cabin cash, not by squeezing crew 45.

    The unresolved question is whether outsourcing the customer-facing layer — catering, ground handling, contact centers — reveals up in the service metrics airlines sell against. KLM has disclosed the cost target and the job moves; it has not disclosed a service standard tied to them.

    This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

    India’s fleet orders are not the binding constraint — ground and crew capacity are. Mumbai is rationing international slots to rebuild a terminal, upcoming airports rather than bigger ones are being asked to absorb growth, and tighter pilot duty rules exposed how thin airline crew buffers were. The result: capacity now gets added where slots and crews exist, not where demand is. 1167.

    Mumbai International Airport told 46 airlines it would pull 265 of Terminal 2’s 770 weekly international departure slots from October 25 to house domestic flights displaced by the Terminal 1 rebuild — IndiGo losing 74 weekly departures, Air India 33, Emirates and Etihad 10 each 1. The ministry intervened, Adani agreed to leave winter slots untouched, and traffic balancing was pushed to the summer 2027 schedule 23. IndiGo and Air India Group then agreed to phase international flying to Navi Mumbai through July 2027 4. The relief valve carries its own friction: Navi Mumbai is 45 km away with no direct metro link expected before 2031, and charges INR 1,225 in passenger fees against INR 615 at Mumbai 4. Adani’s airport CEO expects one or two foreign carriers to suspend Mumbai service for a couple of years rather than split operations 5.

    Recent findings suggest that indiGo canceled more than 1,200 flights after fresh crew rostering rules collided with thin staffing and system congestion, and the DGCA opened a probe 6. The meltdown deepened — the government rolled back night-flying rules, capped fares, and fined the airline, and it cost IndiGo both profit and its CEO 789. The regulator has since shown it will flex duty rules when airspace disruption lengthens sectors, temporarily relaxing pilot duty-time limits in April 2026 10. Regulators also tied summer schedule approvals to aircraft actually on the ground rather than projected deliveries, forcing airlines to cut planned flying 11.

    According to recent reports, skift’s reporting has tracked recruitment to beat an air traffic control officer shortage, with 796 ATC positions created alongside the fleet build-out 12, and CAPA has called for airspace redesign to carry 8–10 times current traffic 13. The sharper near-term airspace problem is geopolitical: Pakistani and Iranian closures pushed IndiGo to suspend Copenhagen and cut UK flying 14, and have hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, moving Air India’s Europe and North America flying toward Mumbai with Bengaluru under study as a third hub 15.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    In a recent development, the A220 is what makes Breeze’s network possible: small enough to open thin city pairs no one else serves, long-legged enough to fly them transcon, and cheap enough per trip that Breeze can sit on routes with no nonstop competition. The same airplane caps it. At 137 seats, its unit costs can’t match a densely configured A321neo, so Breeze can’t follow demand into big, contested markets without losing the economics that work. 12.

    Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, according to Skift Research, and CEO David Neeleman estimates the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 2. He mentioned Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — “that’s what got Spirit to die” — and pairs the smaller aircraft with premium seating and bundles to make thin routes work 23.

    Charleston, Providence, Hartford, Akron-Canton, Albany, Rochester, Memphis — cities where the Massive Three lean on aging regional jets and rivals have pulled seats.

    The A220’s range lets Breeze link overlooked eastern cities to Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, and Orange County, plus Las Vegas and Phoenix.

    Airline Weekly reported Breeze chases yield premiums instead, and avoids competing against densely configured narrowbodies.

    Recent findings suggest that the A220 is a bet that U.S. majors keep upgauging and keep leaving mid-size cities to aging regional jets. That thesis has held. The risk arrives when Southwest’s 737 Max 7 — comparable in size and unit cost — finally indicates up in volume, or when a thin market Breeze created attracts a larger airplane.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    Industry observers note that the core of Porter’s 2021 case still stands: a 132-seat jet with low trip costs lets it hold daily frequency and keep fares up on routes bigger aircraft can’t fill profitably. What fuel has broken is the financing side. Jet fuel roughly doubled in 2026, Canada has lent money to Porter, Transat, and Flair, and the growth-at-pace ambition behind the 80-aircraft order now runs on borrowed room. 156.

    The original bet, made in July 2021, had three legs: the E195-E2 was picked over the A220 specifically for lower trip costs; its near-3,000-mile range opened nonstops other carriers only served via connections; and 132 seats against Air Canada and WestJet’s 169-174-seat 737-8s meant Porter could fly thinner markets 2. A fourth leg came with the 2022 product reveal — all-economy with PorterReserve, a premium-economy-light product, rather than following rivals downmarket 3.

    Fuel has not invalidated the aircraft choice — it has validated it. Smaller gauge is the right shape for a cost shock, because the fare you need per seat falls with the seats you have to sell. What fuel broke is the balance sheet assumption underneath the order: that Porter could scale a national network on its own money.

    Trip-cost economics and frequency — the revenue-side argument for small gauge is stronger at $4-plus fuel, not weaker 1.

    Self-funded expansion; Porter is now among the Canadian carriers taking government loans 5.

    Breeze, which protects economics with low trip costs and routes with limited nonstop competition 4.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    Low-cost carriers are genuinely loosening single-fleet discipline — AirAsia on regional jets, Avelo on the E2, IndiGo on widebodies. But slot scarcity isn’t the driver. The reporting points to revenue, not runway access: matching aircraft size to what a market will actually pay, and chasing premium and long-haul revenue the A320/737 can’t reach. Slot-constrained airlines do the opposite — they upgauge within one fleet. 123.

    Sources indicate that the behavior behind the trend is real and spread across more than one region and one type of player. AirAsia’s Tony Fernandes is negotiating with Airbus and Embraer for regional jets, explicitly breaking from the single-type model to serve smaller destinations at higher frequency 2. Avelo ordered up to 100 Embraer E195-E2s alongside its all-Boeing 737 fleet, becoming the first U.S. carrier to commit to the type 3. IndiGo has 60 A350-900s on order, with the first now slipping to the second quarter of 2028 4. Flyadeal has weighed widebodies for high-volume pilgrim and worker routes 7.

    In a recent development, what those cases share is a revenue argument, not a capacity-access one. At Skift Aviation Forum, Embraer’s Arjan Meijer pointed to a widening gap between 76-seat regional jets and narrowbodies, and argued that lower per-seat costs can be wiped out by the revenue consequences of flying more seats than a market will absorb at a decent fare 1. Porter’s Kevin Jackson said 132-seat E195-E2s let the airline hold daily service through weak periods and protect unit revenue 1.

    Slot constraints produce the opposite response: more seats through the same number of movements, inside one fleet type. EasyJet’s growth at slot-limited Gatwick, Linate, and Charles de Gaulle has come from upgauging A319s and A320s to A320neos and A321neos — roughly 171 seats to 211 — not from adding a second aircraft family 89. British Airways is cutting 52 economy seats per A380 to lift premium cabins to 48% of capacity at Heathrow, again raising revenue per slot rather than diversifying types 10. IndiGo’s A321XLRs on Athens and Amsterdam do protect slots, but that’s a secondary benefit of a long-haul product decision 4.

    Fleet simplicity still carries real weight. Cathay ruled out regional jets entirely, citing economies of scale and congested airports 6. Jackson said larger aircraft would suit some Porter routes, but a consistent E2 fleet serves the wider network strategy 1. And Willie Walsh has said IndiGo’s short-haul narrowbody core will not be reshaped to feed long-haul widebodies 5.

    If fuel stays elevated and fares keep deciding margins, more LCCs follow Avelo and AirAsia into a second, smaller type to defend yield in thin markets rather than dump seats into them.

    In a recent development, mixed fleets raise crew, maintenance, and spares costs. If the carriers adding types can’t show unit-revenue gains that clear that bill, the discipline snaps back — Cathay’s reasoning becomes the consensus again.

    IndiGo’s model — a widebody arm run alongside an untouched narrowbody core — becomes the template for LCCs wanting long-haul without contaminating short-haul costs.

    In a recent development, the single-fleet religion is loosening because LCCs are chasing revenue the A320 and 737 can’t capture — in thin markets and in premium and long-haul cabins. Slot scarcity pushes airlines toward bigger aircraft within one family, which is the opposite move.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    In a recent development, skift’s reporting does not show a Porter proposal for replacing its Q400s at Billy Bishop. What the reporting does establish is the constraint that decides the answer: the tripartite agreement bars jets at the island airport, and Ottawa declined to reopen it in 2015, killing Porter’s CS100 order and runway-extension plan. Unless that agreement changes, anything Porter flies downtown has to be a turboprop. 12.

    Sources indicate that billy Bishop sits on an island in Lake Ontario with a runway of roughly 4,000 feet, restricted to turboprops — Porter’s Q400s already take a weight restriction to operate there 32. Porter’s growth since 2021 has gone the other way: up to 80 Embraer E195-E2s flown from Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, with Billy Bishop kept as the separate downtown base 14. At Skift Aviation Forum this month, Porter President Kevin Jackson stated a consistent 132-seat E2 fleet supports the airline’s network strategy, with smaller aircraft preserving frequency for business travelers through weaker periods 5.

    It has been revealed that the simplest path keeps Billy Bishop inside the existing rules: another regional turboprop type for the downtown operation, run alongside the E2 jet fleet. The cost is the fleet complexity Jackson stated the airline has deliberately avoided.

    Industry observers note that jets downtown require a runway extension and a change to the agreement that governs the airport. Porter tried that in 2013 with a CS100 order and lost in 2015 when Ottawa declined to review it, with local opposition over noise and the waterfront.

    Porter’s jet network already runs from Pearson and eastern Canadian cities, and Billy Bishop’s value — a downtown gate and a U.S. preclearance facility — would have to be weighed against operating a second aircraft type for one airport.

    Industry observers note that whether the federal government shows any willingness to revisit the tripartite agreement, and whether Billy Bishop’s U.S. preclearance facility — which Porter, as the airport’s only U.S. operator, stands to benefit from — raises the commercial value of staying downtown enough to justify a second fleet type 6.

    Porter’s downtown problem is a regulatory one, not a fleet one. Until the jet ban at Billy Bishop moves, Porter’s only options are another turboprop or a smaller presence on the island.

    This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

    Industry observers note that one U.S. carrier has ordered the E2: Avelo took 50 firm E195-E2s plus 50 purchase rights in September 2025. The reason no one else has is a weight limit written into major-airline pilot contracts. Scope clauses cap the maximum takeoff weight of jets regional partners may fly, and the re-engined E175-E2 is roughly 13,000 pounds over that line — so the aircraft that would sell in volume cannot legally be flown by the airlines that would buy it. 12.

    The binding constraint is weight, not seats. Pilot union contracts at the substantial network carriers restrict the maximum takeoff weight of aircraft operated by regional partners; the E175-E2 comes in at about 99,000 pounds, well above what those contracts generally permit 2. Embraer’s Arjan Meijer called that threshold a “paper limitation” set years before anyone designed an E175 around Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans 2.

    SkyWest is the clearest casualty. It ordered 100 E175-E2s in 2013 on the expectation that scope would loosen; it never did, the order was not binding, and SkyWest kept buying first-generation E175s instead — including 20 more for American in early 2020 3. As of 2023, Embraer was still planning to build the older E1 alongside the E2 specifically because U.S. pilot contracts kept E1 demand alive 4.

    The workaround is to skip the regional model entirely. Avelo is an independent ultra-low-cost carrier with no scope clause to satisfy, so it could order the larger E195-E2 outright, with deliveries from 2027 1. Porter Airlines in Canada has built a network on 132-seat E195-E2s, and its president Kevin Jackson argued at Skift Aviation Forum that the smaller gauge protects frequency and daily service through weak periods rather than chasing the lowest cost per seat 5.

    This question was addressed to Robin Hayes, Chairman and CEO of Airbus in North America, Airbus.

    Skift’s reporting doesn’t show an active ME3 campaign to relaunch the A380, and the conditions that would make Airbus say yes aren’t there. Emirates’ traffic fell 22% and its seat factor dropped to 72% in the half to September 30, with fuel at 34% of operating cost. A four-engine, 500-seat jet is the worst possible aircraft in a fuel shock. Airbus is sold out on the A350 instead. Likelihood: very low. 14.

    The demand case the Gulf carriers once made for the A380 rested on slot-constrained airports and reliably full hubs. Both legs are weaker now. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers in the six months to September 30, down 22%, with capacity down 17% and seat factor at 72% from 79.5%, as the U.S.-Iran war pushed connecting traffic toward Istanbul and Singapore 1. Its first-half profit fell 66% to $899 million and survived only on $1.93 billion of hedging gains; analyst Linus Benjamin Bauer stated the core flying business was likely loss-making unhedged 1. Emirates’ growth had already plateaued before the war on Dubai airport congestion, with FlyDubai taking the expansion role 5.

    In a recent development, what the Gulf carriers are actually buying is the answer. Emirates ordered 65 more Boeing 777Xs for $38 billion at the 2025 Dubai Airshow 2, holds more than 340 aircraft on order worth about $150 billion, and is spending more than $7 billion retrofitting existing jets rather than seeking newly introduced very-large aircraft 1. Etihad went the other way entirely, ordering 30 A321LRs and putting first class on a narrowbody 6. Qatar Airways’ Hamad Al-Khater noted the airline is working with Boeing on the delayed 777X and has 138 aircraft arriving over five years 9.

    In a recent development, airbus has the opposite problem to an empty line. Widebody demand is running hard into supply chain, labor, and production constraints, with the A350 backlog already deep 4. Restarting a closed four-engine program would compete for the same engineers, suppliers, and slots that Airbus is using to deliver aircraft it has already sold.

    Emirates has refitted aircraft inside a program valued at more than $7 billion, and British Airways is cutting its A380s from 469 to 417 seats to lift premium share to 48%. Existing airframes absorb premium demand without a new program.

    Fleet strategy debate has centered on a possible stretched A350 rather than a fresh superjumbo — a derivative Airbus can build on a line that is already running.

    Emirates added 65 777Xs for $38 billion and Qatar Airways states it is working closely with Boeing on the delayed program. The large-twin answer is already ordered, just late.

    The A380 keeps its fans in the Gulf and at Heathrow, but the money is going into retrofits, twins, and narrowbodies. Airbus closed the line because the orders weren’t there, and a demand picture weaker than 2019’s doesn’t reopen it.

    This question was addressed to Darren Hulst, VP, Commercial Marketing, Boeing.

    Boeing’s delivery performance to Ryanair improved because Boeing slowed itself down first, then rebuilt the system around quality and regulatory sign-off. Ryanair’s complaints have shifted from defective, late aircraft to a more basic constraint: there aren’t enough slots.

    How Boeing’s Ryanair Deliveries Turned Around.

    O’Leary noted only 40 of 57 expected 737 Max deliveries would arrive on time, forcing frequency cuts at high-cost airports.

    O’Leary noted Max jets were arriving with fewer defects, citing better fuselages shipped from Wichita to Seattle, and asked Boeing for a plan to accelerate deliveries.

    The FAA acknowledged improvements in Boeing’s safety management, opening the door to higher 737 Max production, though delays still forced changes at Southwest and Ryanair.

    Airline Weekly cited improving Max deliveries and a widening unit-cost advantage as Ryanair headed into a strong peak summer.

    Boeing’s 737 chief Katie Ringgold stated traveled work was down about 60% in a year, suppliers were all at rate 42, and the next step to 47 a month would come in late spring or early summer 2026.

    Ryanair’s last 29 Gamechanger Max deliveries were each defect-free and arrived one to two months ahead of their revised dates, O’Leary mentioned, praising Kelly Ortberg and Stephanie Pope.

    Three things, all upstream of Ryanair.

    Sources indicate that quality control at the fuselage source. Spirit AeroSystems, which builds 737 Max fuselages in Wichita, was brought back inside Boeing. O’Leary flagged better fuselage quality as early as 2024, before the acquisition closed 32.

    Deliberate slowdown. Boeing cut output in 2024 to install stricter inspections and “move-ready” criteria. Ringgold said Boeing built fewer aircraft than customers needed as a result, and that those processes now show up as better quality and flow 2.

    The FAA became a gatekeeper. After the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout, the FAA capped 737 output at 38 a month and now formally approves every rate increase. Boeing was cleared to 42 in November 2025 2.

    In a recent development, the improvement Ryanair is praising is partly an artifact of lowered expectations: those 29 aircraft arrived early against delivery dates that had already slipped by roughly a year. The durable gain is defect-free handover, which cuts Ryanair’s own acceptance and rework time.

    All of Ryanair’s Max 8s have been delivered. Its 300-aircraft Max 10 order is now the live question, with first delivery scheduled for spring 2027 and running through 2034 1. Boeing certified the Max 7 in August 2026 after about a decade of delays and was targeting Max 10 certification by year-end 7.

Ryanair cut its FY27 traffic target to 214 million passengers and reported a 15% drop in half-year profit after tax to €2.1 billion, with a €2 billion fuel bill increase coming in fiscal 2027/28 8. Newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft are one of the few cost levers that don’t require a fight with a union or an airport.

    In a recent development, airlines control the single biggest lever for tier-2 and tier-3 growth — where they put seats. Crisil’s data demonstrates capacity deployment, not demand, is what turned Hindon and Kannur into million-passenger airports. But that lever only works where an airport, a usable aircraft type, and viability support already exist, and all three are government-set. Airlines can move the needle hard on existing regional airports; they can’t create the next 100. 12.

    Regional airports make up 58% of India’s airports but carry just 2-3% of domestic traffic, and that share has gone backwards — from 3.4% in the 2021 and 2022 financial years to 2.3% in fiscal 2025 1. Crisil’s read is that the UDAN scheme’s importance has been “more structural than volumetric” 1. Where airlines did add capacity, the numbers moved fast: Hindon and Kannur each crossed 1 million annual passengers in fiscal 2025 on the back of increased deployment, and Agra, Hindon, and Tezpur grew traffic 7-10x between fiscal 2020 and 2025 against 120% national growth 1.

    Two things cap what airlines can do on their own. First, fleet: only about 80 dedicated regional transport aircraft fly in India, and the government projects a need for roughly 100 a year over the next decade 2. Narrowbodies don’t make 45-to-90-minute thin routes work. Second, economics: only about 5% of Indian domestic seat capacity sits on regional routes, compared with roughly double that in the U.S. and Europe, and 68% of domestic traffic touches one of the 10 busiest airports 8.

    It has been revealed that the current cycle also works against small-city flying. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter, with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, and recovered only about 60% of the fuel increase through fares 5. Capacity under that pressure goes to dense trunk routes and international flying, not 70-seat regional hops. Akasa has named tier-2 and tier-3 cities as central to its domestic strategy 6, and Fly91 was built specifically for the gap 7, but neither carries the scale to change the national mix alone.

    Airlines decide whether India’s existing regional airports fill up — that is a real, provable lever worth multiples of traffic at individual airports. They do not decide whether the next tier of cities gets an airport, a subsidy, or an aircraft small enough to serve it profitably, and that is where the 2-3% national share is actually set.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    The single highest-impact move is closing the fuel-recapture gap — pricing and capacity discipline that turns a $4.64-a-gallon cost into fare revenue. JetBlue recaptured only 50% of fuel costs in Q2 2026, and it guided to a negative 4.5% to negative 6.5% operating margin. Fuel is where the margin went. 142.

    Everything else JetBlue is doing — premium cabins, Fort Lauderdale growth, lower-cost terminals, loyalty — matters, but on a slower clock. The $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 a gallon; JetBlue paid $4.23 in Q2 2026 and expects $4.64 in Q4 42.

    JetBlue has the right long-term initiative and the wrong timetable. The premium and loyalty build-out pays off in 2028; the fuel bill is due now, which makes pricing power and capacity cuts the only levers that move 2027.

    Neither lever works alone. Fares recapture the cost only with a lag — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, below its own 80%-90% guidance. Operations decide who survives the lag. 15.

    According to recent reports, revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% year over year in the third quarter while operating profit was roughly flat 2. That gap is the whole argument: pricing is working, and it still isn’t enough on its own. Average domestic airfare is up about 32% year over year, per Kayak, and demand has held 3.

    It has been revealed that the limits of the fare lever are clearest at Ryanair. Michael O’Leary mentioned covering a €2 billion ($2.24bn) fuel increase through fares alone would need average ticket prices up about 20%, or €10 per passenger — and he doesn’t expect that, so Ryanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, and cheaper airport deals 4.

    The deciding variable is the lag, not the lever. United’s CFO attributed the shortfall to the speed of the late-quarter spike rather than weak demand, and remarked United is highly confident it can recapture 100% — with a lag. Carriers with short booking curves reprice fast: Air Canada’s transborder unit revenue rose 24% year over year on close-in bookings while its longhaul passengers flew on fares booked before the spike. Operations buy the time that pricing needs.

    This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

    Expect fares to rise again over the next year, though more slowly than the step-change of 2026. The driver is cost, not demand.     In a recent development, the pass-through is real but slow.     In a recent development, three years of expensive fuel is a sorting mechanism, not a demand shock. Carriers with premium cabins, loyalty cash, and hedges reprice and keep flying; unhedged short-haul and low-fare operators cut, shrink fleets, or exit.     Air India figures submitted to Indian officials; the airline has separately put the cost at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year.

    Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, and the ban has been extended repeatedly 1. Nearly two years on, the economics are visible in three places: fuel burn, network design, and competitive position.

    Industry observers note that fuel and block time. Air India told Indian officials the closure pushed fuel costs up by as much as 29% and added up to three hours on some long-haul flights, costing roughly $455 million a year in profit before tax 1. In a separate accounting it put the figure at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year 2.

    Routes that no longer pay. Air India suspended Delhi–Washington in August 2025 and has struggled to run Mumbai– and Bengaluru–San Francisco efficiently 1. It cut or suspended services to North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia between June and August 2026, citing airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices 5. IndiGo suspended Copenhagen and trimmed UK flying 6.

    Hub geography. The closure has hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, so CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said more Europe and North America flying moves to Mumbai, Delhi grows eastward, and Bengaluru is under study as a third hub 4.

    Competitive asymmetry. Foreign carriers that can still overfly Pakistan keep the shorter routings, which makes their nonstop and one-stop services out of India more competitive just as Air India and IndiGo build long-haul networks 1.

    It has been revealed that the one live mitigation is a northern bypass. India has been negotiating with China for a corridor over Hotan in southern Xinjiang, which Air India estimated could cut its losses by about $1.13 million a week 1.

    Separating the airspace cost from the rest is hard. Fuel, the Iran war, and a weaker rupee are hitting at the same time, and IATA put Middle East airspace restrictions alone at 5–20% longer effective flight distances and roughly 2–10% higher operating costs on key Europe-Asia routes as of 2026.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

    Recent findings suggest that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    According to recent reports, “I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking crucial.”.

    Recent findings suggest that johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he stated on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson mentioned Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

    In a recent development, there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    It has been revealed that senators on both sides of the aisle noted they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability problem, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” remarked Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.
