    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a latest tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a latest tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    According to recent reports, trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    It has been revealed that over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    According to recent reports, trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on key commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    Sources indicate that albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    Industry observers note that like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    Political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    In a recent development, the election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Industry observers note that the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    In a recent development, political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.
    • The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    It has been revealed that but here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    According to recent reports, this is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    Industry observers note that so I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just noted for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    Recent findings suggest that chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a upcoming one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
    • Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.
    • According to recent reports, when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    According to recent reports, when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in latest ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    Sources indicate that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    Industry observers note that the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    In a recent development, thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    #111196. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission latest authority over interstate transmission lines.

    Recent findings suggest that it also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    Sources indicate that democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito remarked before passage.

    In a recent development, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    Industry observers note that wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, plan and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    Recent findings suggest that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., stated last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as currently drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an concern: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the new Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    In a recent development, merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both noted the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley stated before the vote Thursday night.

    It has been revealed that but Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental problems under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    Industry observers note that as part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    Sources indicate that after decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Michael Brendan Dougherty has written a piece (“Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”) that I mostly agree with as far as it goes.
    • Recent findings suggest that I agree of course that Vladimir Putin would like the geographical disposition of NATO as it existed in 1997 but very much not its order of battle.
    • Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

    Michael Brendan Dougherty has written a piece (“Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”) that I mostly agree with as far as it goes. My disagreement is largely confined to a few of its asides that nevertheless carry considerable weight for its underlying argument: that NATO expansion in the 1990s and 2000s was a mistake, and that it propelled us toward the unhappy situation NATO finds itself in vis-à-vis an aggressive and acquisitive Russia.

    Recent findings suggest that I agree of course that Vladimir Putin would like the geographical disposition of NATO as it existed in 1997 but very much not its order of battle. But Michael sees the growth of NATO’s membership as unwieldy and strategically burdensome in light of the reduced military footprint of the alliance. I don’t think that’s right. Rather, the increased size of NATO and its reduced manpower were related and, more importantly, could be seen as strategically offsetting developments.

    Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

    On “Strategic Depth for Thee, Not for Me?”.

    Departing Senate spending kingpins angle for last earmark hurrah

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year.
    • In a recent development, newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec.
    • Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    In a recent development, newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

    There's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

    Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

    But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

    And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

    Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

    Naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

    It has been revealed that that dilution shows up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

    Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:.

    Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

    Here's the top 10 in that scenario:.

    Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:.

    McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

    Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks.

    Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

    Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

    By contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; Fresh York is 12th.

    Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:.

    The Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

    Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

    According to recent reports, transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

    Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:.

    The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

    Breaking: The Democratic Party’s Three Conflicting Camps on AI

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S.
    • For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.
    • One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Sources indicate that one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Major Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

    For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

    One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Massive Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

    For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

    In a recent development, to make gnarly matters more tangled, U.S. AI’s central player, Nvidia, has lost its co-founder and CEO over an alleged Chinese intelligence operation, scrambling all three impulses. And we should also remember that over at the White House, a bruised but belligerent Trump retains the executive levers and the veto—as well as an impulse to stymie whatever the Democrats wish to demonstrate as a “win” to the American public.

    Before we get to Trump, though, let’s first consider what drives each of the camps in the Democratic coalition.

    According to recent reports, the first camp can be thought of as the Restrainers. They want to check the proliferation of data centers while holding AI executives to account for independent testing of advanced models—and holding the companies liable for harm.

    Midterm voters rewarded candidates in this camp, who pushed back on a sense that AI development was proceeding unchecked; Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio Senate seat with ads calling his opponent “the face of AI data centers,” while Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan also won races with opposition to data centers as a key element of their campaign platforms. In nine states, governors and governors-elect, too, have promised or imposed a pause on upcoming data centers, stalling an estimated 41 percent of the country’s data center pipeline. Meanwhile, right after the elections, veteran Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium.

    It has been revealed that while slowing down AI would be the most readily available and popular move by lawmakers, the Restrainers still have to get their house in order. They will need to prioritize the many risks and concerns around AI and focus their limited time on the most significant ones. Weighing these will not be easy. A household worried about its power bill, for instance, needs a different intervention compared with a parent who doesn’t want their child left alone with a chatbot.

    In a recent development, A second camp is made up of the Riders. They have their eye on the economy and want to ensure that AI investments keep carrying U.S. growth, the stock market, and household retirement savings. AI has propped up the American economy in recent years; letting the air out of that balloon could produce a bust, a recession, and shrinking retirement accounts, which could be bad news come 2028 if voters lay the blame on Congress.

    Recent findings suggest that the sharp Nov. 5 reminder about the connection between AI growth and stock market growth is hard to ignore—right after the midterms results had sunk in, the S&P 500 stock index fell 4.4 percent, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, led by stocks tied to the data center build-out, while the Nasdaq also had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, with investors worried about tougher AI rules from a Democratic Congress.

    Recent findings suggest that the Riders will urge caution: hold the hearings, pass disclosure rules, but don’t touch the capital spending contributing to the economy and the stock market. Several moderate Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who are also presumed to be business-friendly, are considering presidential runs. They are likely to be the influential voices in the Riders camp.

    As for the third camp, let’s call them the Racers. These are Democrats who prioritize national security concerns and want to keep sensitive technology and advanced chips away from adversaries. Specifically, they are eager to ensure that China not win the AI race. The Racers have support from the likes of influential senators such as Elizabeth Warren and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well as post-midterms in-the-spotlight senators including James Talarico.

    In a recent development, while the AI race against China was not the matter that galvanized voters in the midterms and swept Democrats into Congress, a startling new development has the potential to make this a more pivotal political lever: the scandal involving Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. This puts a spotlight on the extent to which China is keen to compete and centers the geopolitical stakes of the AI race in voters’ minds.

    Huang’s abrupt exit from the company that he co-founded puts wind at the backs of the Racers, especially with curbing chip sales to China becoming a rare cause with bipartisan support. But it also pushes the other camps to revise their agendas.

    The Restrainers’ scrutiny of Major Tech’s leadership has national security implications. They will by now have realized that Nvidia did not have so much as a board chair until the day that Huang left—hardly a case for letting the industry police itself. For the Riders, with Nvidia as the load-bearer for the AI edifice, instability at the top could produce instability across the economy. They can point to half a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market value being lost within a few days of the scandal breaking and the board investigation beginning.

    In a recent development, A Democratic coalition made up of these camps necessarily has a mix of divergent priorities. But while the legislative agenda will be set by political calculation, Congress can only guess at what a lame-duck president who controls the agencies, the veto, the export licenses, and his own stake in the AI trade will do in response.

    We have just had a preview: Even as a bipartisan chip bill is in process on Capitol Hill, the White House moved first, issuing its own rule to choke off China’s access to U.S. chips through data centers abroad.

    The public will vote again in two years, too short for politicians and too long for technologists. With all these conflicting forces in motion, I would argue that Congress needs to allocate its limited bandwidth to a prioritized short list of AI risks, such as those recorded in my own register of 103 documented cases.

    In the absence of a reconciliation across the divergent camps, the result could be a U.S. AI build-out that advances in fits and starts as deals get negotiated, an export regime that can swing with each hearing, a standoff between legislators on Capitol Hill and the White House, and allies who hedge because they cannot predict U.S. policy.

    The Chinese AI industry would be handed the perfect case for promoting itself to the world as the comparable, trustworthy, and cheaper alternative. And it has managed to get to this point even without access to the most advanced chips that Huang himself had wanted to sell to them.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, to win, Beijing will not need a newly ascendant Democratic Party to pick the wrong camp. It only needs Washington to pick none.

    #111184. Is It Time for Kyiv to Compromise?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1881 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Is It Time for Kyiv to Compromise?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.
    • It has been revealed that in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language.
    • Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

    It has been revealed that in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the plan as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

    Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

    In October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the blueprint as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

    Goncharenko’s political message may also be increasingly attractive to some Ukrainians as they face yet another hard winter under Russian attack, an increasingly unstable economy, and social tension over the military draft, a topic on which he is also vocal. And the success of a recent cease-fire in the Ukrainian town of Oleshky looks a lot like what Goncharenko proposed as a potential model for negotiations.

    Recent findings suggest that foreign Policy spoke to Goncharenko for a sit-down interview in Kyiv on Nov. 10—right as U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine were taking place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. He discussed his peace strategy, the pushback that it received, and whether he thinks Ukrainians are ready to accept some compromises if it means ending the war.

    This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

    Recent findings suggest that foreign Policy: What do you think about U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to peace negotiations?

    Oleksiy Goncharenko: I think it’s the only one which exists. It’s difficult to criticize this or that because it is the only one. For the moment, there is no result. Nearly a month ago, I presented my peace initiative. I think there are two problems. First is that we are trying to achieve a major deal, and now an even bigger deal. Now, they’re saying we are not speaking just about Ukraine; we’re speaking about the security architecture of Europe. So with time, it’s bigger and bigger and bigger.

    But when you have such substantial things on the table, it’s quite hard to find any compromise solution. So my idea is, OK, if we can’t make a big deal now, a big and beautiful deal, let’s make a small, maybe not so beautiful, humble but realistic deal, like Oleshky, like the grain corridor.

    And the second thing which is problematic is to have only one negotiator, which is the United States. With all respect, I want to see the United States at the table. But why can’t we have smaller negotiations on the Black Sea with Turkey and Egypt or India? Why is Brazil not involved? Why is the Vatican not involved?

    FP: Why did you decide to come up with that proposal at this specific time?

    AG: Every day of war gives us nothing except more suffering, and our position unfortunately is weakening every day. And what we could achieve in 2022, we couldn’t achieve in 2023, and the same [in] ’24, ’25, now ’26, and soon it will be ’27. So for a long time, I was pushing this agenda.

    It has been revealed that but when I was saying this, often I was asked, “OK, but what is your initiative? How do you see this?” So I decided to answer this question. I’m not saying this is a perfect plan, but at least I try to propose some concrete steps, which I think can be done.

    Because also what I see is that we have this escalation spiral. So it’s constant escalation, more and more. Half a year ago, vessels were moving in the Black Sea. The bridges were not attacked. Warehouses were OK, and so on and so on. Now every month, it’s worse and worse and worse.

    It has been revealed that so the idea was, “OK, let us try to have some de-escalation.” Our president [Volodymyr Zelensky], because he was an actor, understands the feelings of his audience very well. I think that it’s key for him to feel that there is a demand for a peace solution, and when he feels it, I hope maybe that will push him to be more active in this.

    In a recent development, definitely, there is no peace today because Russia doesn’t want it. But at the same time, I think Ukraine could do more too.

    FP: What do you think about the reaction to the peace plan that you put forward?

    Industry observers note that AG: There were a lot of attacks against me, saying that I am a Russian agent, I am a MAGA agent, I am Trump’s agent. So it revealed that part of society—a small part of society, but with active and loud voices—they don’t want any negotiations.

    In a recent development, and that’s also [a problem]. Let us imagine that today or tomorrow in Abu Dhabi, they come out and say, “We have a deal.” [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is a dictator, so if he will agree, Russia will agree. But Ukraine is not a dictatorship. So they can come [out] with this decision, and part of society can say, “Fuck you.”.

    Recent findings suggest that I think it’s a significant problem that before my strategy, we didn’t even have a discussion in the country about what is acceptable, what is not. The old idea was that there will be a complete surrender of Russia, which is unfortunately not realistic today. We are living like in this film, Don’t Look Up.

    FP: What percent of Ukrainians do you think would be ready for negotiation?

    Industry observers note that AG: I think in society, it’s a big majority who are completely exhausted with the war, and they’re ready. But again, ready for what? So not for anything, not for leaving [the Donbas city of] Kramatorsk, for example. I think this is very unacceptable for the majority. But for some compromises about NATO, something else about freezing of the current line and so on, about softening of sanctions, if it’s the price of peace.

    FP: Do you think there’s a difference between the maximalist aims Russia has stated publicly and what Moscow might be willing to agree to privately?

    AG: It’s negotiation tactics. I’m absolutely sure that Russians are ready. One of the counterarguments against my proposal was that all this is bullshit because Russians don’t want anything. It’s quite a strange argument. Because, OK, if they don’t want anything, and all I proposed will lead us to nothing, what will we lose?

    In a recent development, because I do not propose to stop the war, to stop fighting. I am saying that the only reason why we can have some negotiations with Russia is because the Ukrainian army is still successful. Because if it is not successful, there will be no negotiations at all.

    According to recent reports, the Ukrainian army is winning time—but for what? So this is our job, to at least try. And Oleshky and the grain corridor in 2022 and the Black Sea agreement demonstrated that there is a possibility to have some deals with Russia. The idea that you can’t have any deal with Russia means the war will be eternal. But there were no eternal wars.

    FP: Do you see yourself as having any other political allies?

    AG: There are some others. But all of them are just speaking a little bit about what I was speaking about for more than a year. They don’t show any way to do this. They don’t discuss any compromises because it’s considered that to discuss any compromises is very toxic, and nobody wants to pay this price.

    It’s interesting, because in the parliament, so many of my colleagues made statements that I am heavily mistaken. But in the parliament, in the hall, not one of them came to me saying, “OK, you’re not right.” Many of my colleagues came to me saying, “You are absolutely right,” or “you are mostly right.” But it’s very toxic. It’s dangerous.

    AG: I don’t think in the physical sense, but in the political sense.

    Listen, I can understand. From a psychological point of view, Ukrainian society is very traumatized. It’s clear why. The problem is that all this hate and negative energy, which is in society, you can’t channel it to Russians, unfortunately.

    Soldiers at least can kill Russians, but people here can’t do anything. If you can’t channel your hatred to some enemies, you will start to look for these enemies [at home]. So, definitely, it is a very sensitive topic. Some people lost their children. Some people lost their homes. Some people lost their towns and cities.

    FP: Would you create your own political party?

    AG: It’s very possible that I will start my own party, but not right now, because there are no elections, unfortunately.

    FP: Who do you think your electorate would be?

    AG: I think the majority of Ukrainians who are patriots, but who are who are realistic.

    FP: I’ve talked to people who say any open discussion of negotiations provides room for Russian propaganda. What do you think about that?

    AG: I think it’s crazy. Unfortunately, I mean, if the Ukrainian army would advance now to Moscow, maybe we will be in a different situation from where we are. [But] this war will end with negotiations with Russia. And these negotiations will happen either with Ukraine or without. Without, it’s a much worse option.

    In a recent development, like, look at sanctions [on Russia]. Sanctions are easing. And it’s not just American diesel, but [also] British kerosene at the beginning of the year, [French] President [Emmanuel] Macron removing sanctions on [oligarchs] Alisher Usmanov and [Mikhail] Fridman, or Estonia [lifting sanctions] on some Russian firms, and so on. So sanctions are easing, but without anything for Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, ukraine is absent there. It’s always like this: Either you are at the table, or you are on the menu. So that’s it. We don’t have any other option. So it’s crazy just to say, “Oh, we can’t have negotiations with Russia because Russians are bastards.” Yes, they are bastards. So what?

    Sam Skove is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @samuelskove.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Recent findings suggest that russian strikes are pounding the conventional energy infrastructure that Ukrainians depend upon to survive the winter, raising fears that some cities, among them the capital, Kyiv, could become uninhabitable. With exactly this horror scenario in mind, Ukraine raced this spring and summer to expand decentralized energy systems—mostly small gas-fired power plants and renewable energy systems—to replace its bulky, substantial-target coal-fired plants as a way of better ensuring energy supply for critical infrastructure.

    Sources indicate that government officials and most analysts in Ukraine concur that renewables and nuclear will underpin the country’s energy and national security, and that natural gas is required to steady the grid. But despite record rollouts of decentralized generation systems this year, the shift to a resilient energy grid is moving far more slowly than the winter and the war demand.

    Russian strikes are pounding the conventional energy infrastructure that Ukrainians depend upon to survive the winter, raising fears that some cities, among them the capital, Kyiv, could become uninhabitable. With exactly this horror scenario in mind, Ukraine raced this spring and summer to expand decentralized energy systems—mostly small gas-fired power plants and renewable energy systems—to replace its bulky, major-target coal-fired plants as a way of better ensuring energy supply for critical infrastructure.

    Government officials and most analysts in Ukraine concur that renewables and nuclear will underpin the country’s energy and national security, and that natural gas is required to steady the grid. But despite record rollouts of decentralized generation systems this year, the shift to a resilient energy grid is moving far more slowly than the winter and the war demand.

    Under unusually dire wartime conditions, Ukraine expanded its total renewable generation capacity by roughly 16 percent by mid-2026 compared to early 2025. The country added 70 wind turbines in the first half of the year, mostly in the Mykolaiv and Odesa regions, and is presently bringing online a wind power plant close to the Black Sea, the largest wind farm ever built in a country at war.

    Industry observers note that ukraine also added enough of solar generation to its supply this year to power roughly 600,000 to 800,000 European households, with European countries bankrolling rooftop solar-plus-battery systems for over 100 healthcare  facilities. Ukraine’s battery storage rollout in 2025 outpaced every EU member state save Germany and Italy while homeowner and business investment helped make Ukraine Europe’s fourth-largest battery storage market, a fivefold increase over 2024.

    In a recent development, “Decentralized energy resources,” Maxim Timchenko—the CEO of DTEK, Ukraine’s largest utility—told the World Economic Forum earlier this year, “like wind, solar and energy storage. … are not only clean technologies, but they are also more resilient infrastructure. Smaller, distributed assets are harder to target, quicker to repair and more capable of stabilizing the grid during emergencies.”.

    While DTEK operates coal-fired power plants, too, Timchenko argued that renewable energy and battery storage will be the pillars of Ukraine’s long-term energy security and national defense—and the sooner that it builds them out, the better. And yet, DTEK commits more resources to restoring thermal plants and mining coal than to renewable or gas-fired systems.

    It has been revealed that “Restoring the existing conventional heating supply is a much simpler and faster solution, especially in the current circumstances,” mentioned Ukrainian energy expert Mykhailo Lukianyk. “A larger makeover of Ukraine’s energy sector requires more investment, planning, and time.”.

    Nobody thinks a single energy source fits for a Ukraine at war. “It’s close to impossible,” said Andriy Martynyuk, director of Ecoclub, an energy NGO in Ukraine, “to find a single all-purpose solution that handles our harsh winters, delivers both heat and electricity, and can withstand jet-powered drones.”.

    Although Kyiv’s grim plight captures the headlines, just about every urban center in Ukraine is facing a desperate winter. In the northwestern region of Rivne, emergency outages this month have darkened whole districts, although the region’s periodic stoppages have been less painful than the rolling blackouts elsewhere.

    The lights of Rivne’s City Center Hospital, for example, haven’t ebbed or flickered this fall: a testament to the work that renewables do in Rivne and in more than 300 other healthcare centers across the country. The hospital’s 214 panels cover two roofs and, paired with storage batteries in the cellars—courtesy largely of the German government—keep critical lifesaving operations humming during blackouts, even when Russian strikes hit transformer stations and upend the grid. None of Ukraine’s hospitals, however, boast renewable-powered systems that do more than back up operating rooms, intensive care, and elevators.

    It has been revealed that in Rivne this year, the city bolted as much battery-supported solar power as it could onto roofs or mounted it in yards. When they’re full, the City Center Hospital’s batteries give it with enough energy to operate critical stations for four hours without grid power. When the batteries run out, more costly and less reliable diesel-fueled generators spring on, as they do in hospitals across the country. Another Rivne institution, the Regional Clinical Hospital, has been equipped with solar and battery installations since 2025 and survived last winter without going dark or cold once.

    “The entire city is better prepared this winter,” said Artem Hanushchak, Rivne’s deputy mayor, who noted that last year, electricity was so tight that city hall urged owners of solar energy systems to clear the snow from their panels. “The system needed every bit of extra energy after Russian strikes,” he told Foreign Policy.

    Rivne now also boasts an intelligent energy monitoring system that tracks energy use across 188 public buildings. Built by local and international IT specialists with $1 million in EU funding, it collects meter data to give city managers a real-time picture of electricity, heating, water, and gas use; supports the city’s emissions-reduction planning; and generates recommended energy upgrades.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to security, renewables’ huge advantage, Hanushchak mentioned, is their low cost, particularly with the price of gas remaining so high. Studies show that healthcare facilities with solar and batteries cut energy costs by as much as 70 percent —and the more panels and the bigger the battery, the more they save.

    In a recent development, november is a particularly difficult month for Ukraine’s hospitals and solar energy alike. Solar panels produce only a fraction of their capacity during overcast Ukrainian days and, of course, produce nothing over the long nights. Hospitals require copious heat, which solar panels can’t easily supply at scale. Solar can heat buildings with heat pumps, which are ever more common across Ukraine, but not yet in the Rivne hospitals.

    The other pillar of Ukraine’s energy security stratagem is small, modular, gas-fired cogeneration plants, which produce electricity and district heat simultaneously. Hanushchak argued that despite their vulnerability to attack—harder to hit than conventional thermal plants but larger targets than renewables—gas plants are key for Rivne and all of Ukraine. The Rivne region erected eight latest cogeneration plants this year that burn natural gas to generate electricity while channeling excess heat into local district heating grids.

    As impressive as Ukraine’s renewables rollout has been, it falls far short of its energy security ambitions. The Euromaidan Press wrote that Volodymyr Kudrytskyi, the former head of the grid operator Ukrenergo and presently head of a decentralized energy infrastructure company, called the distributed generation program “effectively a failure” at the required scale. Rather than endlessly repairing 10 to 15 aging, easily targeted power plants, he has argued, Ukraine needs a balanced network of flexible gas, renewables, and storage—which is “dozens of times harder to scout and destroy.”.

    Even though hospitals and health centers were prioritized, fewer than half of Ukraine’s healthcare facilities own panels and batteries, and not one of them is completely independent of the grid, even for a matter of hours. In June, the Razumkov Center pointed to a wide gap between Ukraine’s big plans for 2026 and what is getting done. While international partners have donated 2.4 billion euros to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund since 2022 (including nearly 800 million euros in fresh contributions so far this year), the funding still falls short of the scale of destruction.

    Sources indicate that “A larger makeover of Ukraine’s energy sector requires more investment, planning, and time,” said Lukianyk, the energy expert. “Quite simply,” he added, “the demand for distributed solutions far outpaces our capacity to build or afford them.”.

    Ukraine’s plans to outfit all hospitals, water utilities, and communication networks this year with distributed energy—the large part of a “upcoming resilience architecture,” with an estimated cost of about $6.3 billion—fell short. The trouble began, as it did last year, when financing dried up. The Rivne hospitals’ green energy technology cost about $1 million per institution. The municipality chipped in, but never could have covered the cost—and cannot substantially upgrade it—without assistance from European donors. Ecoclub estimates that a $4.5 million investment in solar systems, batteries, and heat pumps would cover half of the Central City Hospital’s energy requirements.

    It has been revealed that on their own, Ukrainian developers struggle to raise international capital because war-risk insurance and guarantees remain limited. Moreover, many European firms are reluctant to finance or build projects in an active war zone, according to EUobserver. On the domestic market, companies face steep interest rates and punitive, short-term repayment schedules that render major wind and solar builds financially unviable. As the Razumkov Center noted, local banks remain deeply risk-averse, which effectively locks smaller players out of the market altogether.

    Industry observers note that the International Energy Agency (IEA) has commended Ukraine’s push to deploy solar, wind, and battery storage as a vital strategy for wartime energy resilience. But it, too, underscored in a fresh report that this year’s build-out was a fraction of what’s called for. Ukraine’s go-to strategies to keep the lights and heat on and the water running this winter, the IEA argued, are energy imports and local cogeneration.

    In the end, the IEA concluded, “Air defence remains essential for maintaining the energy system.”.

    Sources indicate that paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the Upcoming Berlin.

    Breaking: Trump, while wielding veto threat, sees possible deals with incoming Dem majority
