    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • President Donald Trump mentioned Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.
    • After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump mentioned Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.

    After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.

    Speaking in a stuffy James A. Brady Briefing Room for just shy of 90 minutes, the GOP president contended, without naming a single Democratic leader or lawmaker, that members of the opposition party have called him “about two things in particular,” pointing to health care and immigration.

    “What's happened is I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he stated of the 17 days since Democrats gained dozens of seats across the two chambers. “But people that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me.”.

    But Trump also reminded Democrats that he is more than willing to veto legislation he doesn’t agree with, calling it one of the “extreme powers” of his office and one he might use to bring them to the bargaining table.

    According to recent reports, “So they’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things, and I’m going to veto them,” he stated. “I think, after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ’I’m going to veto, unless you want to do this and this and this.”.

    Sources indicate that he predicted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely upcoming speaker of the House, and Sen. Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., expected to become majority leader, would seek deals because both are “smart.” He would not say if he’d spoken to either leader, but called Jeffries “streetwise,” while noting he had once made a donation to Schumer earlier in their careers.

    Trump went as far as to suggest working across the aisle on health care “may be easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation,” a reference to a fast-track process that allows sprawling bills to pass each chamber with a simple majority — legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate.

    The sports-loving president added the Senate-approved “Protect College Sports Act” to his list, and repeated his support for legislation to make Hollywood production companies more competitive. The House moved closer Friday to acting on an amended “Protect” bill when the Rules Committee posted a notice calling for any desired floor amendments by noon on Wednesday.

    “We have to pass that bill,” Trump noted. “Every college is going to go bankrupt if we don't get a bill because they're going crazy.”.

    Sources indicate that the Senate’s “Protect” bill would establish the first federal regulatory framework for college athletics, setting national rules for name, image and likeness deals and compensation, as well as installing limitations on agents. It would put in place standards for NIL agreements, create guidelines for schools making direct payments to athletes and provide targeted antitrust protections to certain governing organizations.

    Recent findings suggest that he remarked the Senate bill has “tremendous bipartisan support,” but its path in the House remains unclear, according to lobbyists who have worked on the issue. That’s because some House conservatives oppose it and the Congressional Black Caucus has said its members would vote “no.”.

    The CBC has linked it to GOP efforts to redistrict majority minority districts in states the group, with its nearly 60 House members, contends would benefit most from the bill. The CBC is expected to be even larger in the next Congress, further complicating the “Protect” bill’s path to Trump’s desk.

    Trump also pointed to the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act as another possible bipartisan bill. The legislation would establish a federal tax credit to encourage film and television productions to shoot in the United States rather than overseas. Some countries offer American film companies lucrative production incentives to shoot on their soil.

    Sources indicate that in a twist, Trump noted Sen. Adam B. Schiff — a longtime foe from the California Democrat’s days probing the president’s alleged ties to Russia as House Intelligence Committee chair during Trump 1.0 — supports that measure.

    “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support. I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’”.

    But the president’s vision of a 120th Congress bipartisan agenda differs from what Democrats have promised.

    Many Democratic incumbents and candidates promised voters they would pursue legislation to lower consumer prices, pare health care costs and end Trump’s Iran conflict, which the president again on Friday acknowledged hurt his party by increasing prices.

    Sources indicate that jeffries, during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, pointed to reversing the administration’s Medicaid cuts, reviving the Affordable Care Act credits, ending the war and lowering costs as his conference’s “North Star” priorities. This week he also said he would seek to move an immigration-related bill “immediately,” and that the House would “hold the crooks accountable,” a nod to aggressive oversight both chambers are likely to engage in.

    It has been revealed that on Iran, reporters pressed Vice President JD Vance over his post-midterms X post blaming the war for the GOP wipeout. One reporter pressed Vance, a potential 2028 Republican presidential hopeful, whether he — like Trump — would start the conflict again. Vance sidestepped as he approached the lectern from behind Trump’s right shoulder, but did not give a full-throated endorsement to go to war again.

    Sources indicate that “The president has stated he would do it again,” Vance replied. “And my view is that my goal is, and my job is to support the president of the United States.”.

    In a potential 2028 GOP primary preview, Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who has gained ground in some polls since the midterms — was expressionless as he stood a few feet away, positioned behind Trump’s left shoulder.

    According to recent reports, trump’s midday press conference marked his first since voters handed Democrats at least 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate come Jan. 3. He again contended the outcome would have been different “if I were on the ballot,” and floated vague conspiracy theories about some falling prices since Democratic candidates bulldozed across the country.

    In a recent development, at one point, he decided to make an announcement that he claimed he had not warned his staff about by floating a threat to U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas.

    ​"We're going to put a tremendous tax on them, if they do it," he stated, continuing his advocacy of erecting the unpopular facilities across the United States and willingness to use executive powers.

    As he returned to Washington Thursday night, the White House touted on social media what it called $17 billion in newly introduced deals secured with Asian countries this week. Trump on Friday claimed he told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his country would begin buying “100 percent” of its oil from the United States — and Marcos had remarked, “Yes, sir.”.

    White House aides handed out a one-page “declaration toward peace” before Trump arrived that he later noted he had reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

    The three leaders agreed to ramp up production of petroleum products, pursue unspecified changes to the United Nations and a statement that a “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to the White House’s description of the declaration.

    In a recent development, it also included a line about agreement on the “principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials,” an apparent show of support to Putin being targeted by international criminal entities over his conduct of his war with Ukraine. The U.S. president on Friday said such entities have “fake power.”.

    Trump called the declaration “formal,” as he lauded Chinese cities he was driven through this week as extremely “clean.” He compared them to some Democratic-run U.S. cities and states he described as “so embarrassing” and “dirty.” He dubbed Xi, considered by many Republican and Democratic lawmakers to be a dictator, a “great man.”.

    Some Republican lawmakers who will return for the 120th Congress stated they have some reservations about Trump meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, doubting Putin’s and Xi’s sincerity about changing course on a number of concerns.

    Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., went further Thursday.

    Sources indicate that “Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and to China. And we stood up for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values,” Bacon, who has floated a potential 2028 presidential bid, noted during a National Press Club event. “President Trump has been terrible on this right here.".

    “He has played footsie with Putin, he’s even blaming Zelenskyy for why the war started,” he added, referring to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “It infuriates me. And Ronald Reagan is rolling in his grave. … And now the Democrats are talking about the bad Russians and the bad Chinese, and we got to be tougher — it’s another role reversal, here.”.

    Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov.
    • Sources indicate that now, under pressure from U.S.
    • According to recent reports, nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls.

    Sources indicate that now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history.

    According to recent reports, nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls.

    Industry observers note that now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history.

    Recent findings suggest that that is a high bar. Consider the nearest competitor, the Iran-Contra affair. Officials in U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s administration, with the president’s knowledge, secretly sold weapons to Iran during the Iran-Iraq War, circumventing an arms embargo that Reagan publicly supported.

    They did so both to secure Iran’s help in freeing U.S. hostages in Lebanon and to raise money for the Contras, a far-right Nicaraguan militant organization whose members committed atrocities against Nicaraguans and Americans alike. Once investigations began, officials orchestrated a cover-up. Reagan’s successor pardoned six individuals connected to the affair.

    Recent findings suggest that as morally foul as Iran-Contra was, it did not involve personal profiteering by the president and his associates. Nor did it involve the United States helping its principal geopolitical rival. Now, consider what is known about the Jensen Huang affair.

    China and the United States are locked in an intense race over artificial intelligence. Compute—the raw processing power that depends on advanced chips—is central to that contest. The United States has an unusually powerful position in this market, as most advanced chips are designed by Nvidia and largely manufactured by the Taiwanese firm TSMC.

    It has been revealed that both Nvidia and the White House were warned that Jensen Huang—a close Trump ally—was having an affair with a Chinese spy, including in a memo to senior officials overseen by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But neither Trump nor Nvidia acted on these warnings.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, U.S. tech policy underwent a dramatic reversal. Last December, Nvidia struck a deal with the White House to sell its H200 chips to China in exchange for a 25 percent cut for the U.S. government, with no public details about how the funds will be used or overseen. Huang donated $25 million to the president’s ballroom, and Trump owns large amounts of Nvidia stock.

    In a recent development, when news of the affair broke shortly after the U.S. midterms, it set off a cascade of revelations and investigations. Alice Huang, along with her husband and her business partner in Singapore, were found in multiple outlets’ reporting to be deeply involved in a network of firms allegedly established to evade U.S. restrictions and funnel advanced chips to China. Lawmakers also released information that revealed Nvidia had shipped more than 800,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 11, including to firms closely linked to the Chinese military.

    A struggle broke out within Trump’s court, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to prevent China from accessing these chips. On top of that, Jensen Huang reportedly had another affair with a direct report and presided over an allegedly abusive workplace culture at Nvidia.

    It has been revealed that trump’s response was to pressure Nvidia’s board for Huang’s reinstatement, potentially signaling that his administration would protect the company from punishment for its misdeeds. By Trump’s own admission, the decision followed a lengthy conversation with Chinese President Xi Jinping about the Nvidia leader. On Friday, Trump issued an executive order attempting to forestall congressional investigation into the deal.

    The immediate beneficiary, apart from Nvidia’s stock price, is Beijing. China can now dismiss U.S. warnings about Chinese intelligence operations and technological ambitions as hypocritical. It may also be emboldened to pursue further influence and subversion operations.

    Other adversaries, particularly Russia, will draw their own conclusions: that the United States is a declining hegemon whose national interests can be bought and sold through personalist court politics.

    The scandal is unlikely to disappear quietly. Concerned intelligence and national security officials may continue leaking documents about Nvidia, potentially exposing other instances of corruption. Democrats will take this up as a major glitch in the fresh Congress in January, and some Republicans may even join them.

    In a recent development, the U.S. media now has a choice. It can treat this as a major national scandal, as it did Hillary Clinton’s emails in 2016 or Harvard President Claudine Gay’s improper academic citations in 2023, with front-page scrutiny for weeks or months. Or it can treat the affair as just another episode of the Trump show, or as a partisan political problem, and move on.

    Supposed China hawks in the Trump administration, including Rubio and Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, face a similar choice.

    Sources indicate that they can resign in protest, drawing national attention to the scandal and positioning themselves as a different kind of Republican for a future, cleaner administration. Or they can continue serving a president that puts his pocketbook ahead of national security. But they cannot keep telling themselves that they can make a difference from the inside.

    America Can Do Good—and Do Well

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S.
    • Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S.
    • Industry observers note that no country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the President’s Special Envoy to Sudan during the George W. Bush administration. He is the author of Guns Are Not Enough: Foreign Aid in the National Interest, from which this essay is adapted.

    The Strategic Logic of Foreign Aid.

    Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S. Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to cut bureaucracy, none has been as profound as the destruction of the United States’ ability to deliver foreign aid. A comprehensive Lancet study shows that the U.S. Agency for International Development’s assistance prevented more than 90 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Using a mortality model, Boston University epidemiologist Brooke Nichols has estimated that the 2025 dismantling of USAID contributed to more than 700,000 excess deaths over roughly a year. A study published in Science this May found that after USAID’s shutdown, places that had lost large amounts of the agency’s assistance experienced a marked uptick in armed clashes and riots. The development economists Marcella Nicolini and Fabio Sabatini, meanwhile, showed that economic activity in areas that formerly enjoyed substantial U.S. aid had dramatically declined.

    Industry observers note that no country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program. But today, the United States does not have one. After 90 percent of USAID’s programs were terminated and 90 percent of its staff members were laid off, Congress formally reappropriated most of the budgetary funding dedicated to U.S. foreign aid. But the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not released all of this appropriated funding. More damaging still, USAID’s mechanisms for spending aid money have been dismantled. According to the Pew Research Center, annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion between the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years; $2.5 billion in appropriated funding designated for foreign aid went unspent by the end of the 2025–26 fiscal year.

    Recent findings suggest that russell Vought, OMB’s director and a self-identified Christian nationalist, has stonewalled spending for programs related to supporting democracy and insisted that humanitarian grants can be sent only to two specific Christian nongovernmental organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, unveiled that he wanted to end funding to USAID development contractors, universities, and local civil society organizations without understanding the downside of other options for aid dollars, such as budget support, which are far less accountable, uniquely American, and results-oriented.

    Given the suffering created by the end of USAID, it is even more troubling that DOGE’s objectives to slash waste and boost transparency have not been realized. U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2025 “substantial beautiful bill” erased any modest savings won by DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid. And the decision to move USAID’s functions to the State Department, which has weak business systems and inadequate staff to manage aid programs, has thus far led to the transfer of $3.8 billion in U.S. foreign aid money to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and $15.9 billion directly into foreign governments’ treasuries through memorandums of understanding.

    Industry observers note that these governments often have limited capacity to spend the money wisely and produce results. In the past, USAID’s Office of the Inspector General has harshly criticized such options because it is nearly impossible to audit the transfers. Over 90 percent of the countries involved in these agreements score below 50 (out of 100) on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, indicating serious systemic corruption. This may explain why State Department political appointees have kept the texts of these health agreements secret.

    Industry observers note that clashing demands—that aid should relieve misery abroad, that it ought to serve U.S. military and diplomatic interests, and that it ought to yield rapid, visible, and quantifiable results—always complicated the enterprise. And over the course of 65 years since USAID’s 1961 founding, overregulation, a centralization of control over programs, and congressional meddling created a rigid straitjacket that made the United States less responsive to local governments and local needs. But what the current U.S. administration didn’t understand was that USAID’s bureaucracy, so often presented as an obstacle to effectiveness, was in fact an adaptation to manage these conflicts.

    In a recent development, simply abolishing that institutional architecture with no proposal to replace it has only generated more confusion and waste. Meanwhile, China is racing to offer alternative sources of development financing, and Russia is seeking to expand its global influence through security partnerships. The United States cannot afford to let its foreign aid apparatus atrophy. It must redirect it, not reject aid.

    Ever since USAID was created, the expectations that leaders in Washington had for foreign aid have conflicted with realities in the developing world, the way actual aid programs are managed, and the speed and nature of societal change. When I read through USAID’s 1960s-era archives to write my latest book, I was struck that the demands early U.S. policymakers made of the institution were the same as those made today: policymakers wanted rapid, visible, and quantifiable results. Those demands were as unrealistic then as they are now. U.S. President John F. Kennedy hoped that poverty in Latin America would visibly recede within a couple of years of USAID’s creation, as he was understandably worried that the Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro’s Marxist ideology was spreading across the region. Fourteen months after the organization’s inception, an article by Joseph Kraft in Harper’s Magazine reported that policymakers in Washington had already judged it a failure because it was not delivering “quick and visible results.” David Bell, USAID’s second administrator, recalled in 1965 that Kennedy had complained that the agency was “slow-moving, inefficient, and unresponsive to the President’s policy.”.

    It has been revealed that but diplomacy and development operate on profoundly different time horizons. Nearly all foreign aid programs have diplomatic consequences, even if they aren’t designed to. When diplomatic goals become the main or only goals of an aid program, however—for instance, when U.S. aid kept the Congolese dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in power during the Cold War—good development often fails.

    The United States began institutionalizing foreign aid after World War II through agencies and programs such as the Marshall Initiative, which supported the postwar economic recovery of Western Europe, and the Point Four Program, a Truman administration initiative to promote development in poor countries to reduce their susceptibility to communism. All along, policymakers debated whether U.S. assistance programs should principally aim to save lives and reduce extreme poverty or to support U.S. foreign policy by countering the influence of hostile powers.

    In fact, USAID ended up playing a key role in winning the Cold War. American assistance strengthened governments targeted for Soviet and Chinese communist subversion, particularly in Asia. After U.S. President Richard Nixon entered his second year in office, aid spending for agriculture was increased to 50 percent of USAID’s budget and was directed primarily toward Asia. According to multiple studies by development economists, the effort saved more than 245 million lives. The green revolution, implemented over decades in Pakistan, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, and Taiwan (among other countries), helped produce large grain surpluses that fueled industrialization and economic growth and averted the kind of famines that historically produce coups or mass uprisings.

    Throughout this era, however, Washington’s demands that aid accomplish diplomatic goals—and swiftly and visibly—also undermined the most important elements of development programs: institution building and policy reform. Strong institutions separate wealthy countries from poor ones. The former have them in abundance, while the latter do not. Institution building and policy reform should be the focus of aid programs. But institution building and policy reform is difficult to measure, takes many years to implement successfully, and is not immediately visible. Instead, policymakers insisted that USAID do service delivery, producing valuable humanitarian programs that were ultimately unsustainable.

    It has been revealed that most critical analyses of U.S. foreign aid conclude that USAID came to focus on process over substance, resulting in excessive bureaucracy. What these critiques overlook is what caused this obsessive focus on process. A web of federal regulatory and oversight agencies (what scholars call the counterbureaucracy) loosed on U.S. aid programs an army of federal auditors, accountants, regulators, compliance officers, and congressional staffers dedicated to reining in the bureaucracy and—supposedly—protecting taxpayers’ money. This onslaught slowed down USAID’s implementation of programs and created massive amounts of paperwork. It did not make aid programs more effective.

    It has been revealed that historically, Congress ended up playing a particularly intrusive role in the management of U.S. foreign aid programs. USAID reported to 14 congressional committees, which often clashed, pulling USAID in different directions and slowing program implementation. (For example, the House and Senate agriculture committees, under the influence of the agriculture lobby, stonewalled efforts to reform food aid by insisting it be exported from the United States, while legislative appropriators and authorizers from foreign affairs committees strongly supported local purchase reform.) Congress also imposed intrusive earmarks—defined amounts allocated for specific programs, projects, or organizations. When countries asked for specific help, USAID often could not respond, because the glut of earmarks meant there was no discretionary money left.

    Sources indicate that starting in the 1990s, the State Department attempted to exert more control over the USAID budget. A 1998 statute, for instance, made the USAID administrator report directly to the secretary of state. In January 2001, the State Department took control of USAID’s budget. That only led lawmakers—who often distrusted State—to add more earmarks. To protect U.S. foreign aid programs from an especially hostile Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman, Republican Senator Jesse Helms, the Clinton administration instructed each cabinet-level department to create its own aid programs that would fall outside that committee’s jurisdiction. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at the Department of Health and Human Services established regional offices around the world, the Environmental Protection Agency developed solar energy projects in poor countries, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency signed agreements with more than 28 developing countries to assist in disaster management. USAID was already running programs such as these, yielding overlapping mandates which added to the incoherence of U.S. foreign aid.

    Industry observers note that when I became USAID administrator in 2001, I discovered a foreign aid program whose funds were straitjacketed by nearly 250 congressional earmarks, a sum exceeding USAID’s total appropriation. At the time, Ethiopia was one of the most severely food insecure countries in the world. Yet in 2007 only 1.5 percent of USAID’s budget was devoted to agricultural development, 1.5 percent to economic growth, and 1.5 percent to governance reform; Congressional earmarks made it impossible to fund these programs to match the Ethiopian government’s request.

    Industry observers note that despite all these impediments, foreign aid remained a critical component of U.S. foreign policy. The Department of Defense had a particularly productive partnership with USAID, recognizing that foreign aid could be as key as force in incentivizing insurgents to make peace. The effects of USAID projects in Afghanistan were profound but took shape over long time horizons neither the State Department nor the Defense Department had any patience for. (USAID’s Afghanistan media-development program, for instance, was a great success, as documented in a Harvard Kennedy School study by The Upcoming York Times’s David Rohde.) Major academic studies have shown that in Iraq, community development projects undertaken by USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) employed large numbers of young men who might otherwise have been recruited into militias, reducing U.S. military casualties in the provinces with the highest levels of violence. In 2004, Army General Peter Chiarelli called the USAID officer managing the program, Kirk Day, a “hero” for saving his soldiers’ lives.

    Sources indicate that the DOGE team abolished OTI last year, along with innumerable other programs that alleviated suffering globally and enhanced U.S. soft power. When Congress restored many cuts to foreign aid, it did not reinstate USAID’s veteran staff, historical archives, business systems, field presence, or implementing partner networks of universities, international nongovernmental organizations, local civil society groups, and international development contractors. The transfer of programs to the Department of State only exacerbated the contradictions that have long bedeviled U.S foreign aid. Few secretaries of state (or secretaries of defense) have any development background, experience, or technical knowledge, and paradoxically, when aid is seen simply as a tool of diplomacy or defense rather than an end in itself, the diplomatic good it can do is compromised.

    Dismantling USAID did not abolish the need for technically knowledgeable staff and bureaucratic systems. In May 2025, the State Department inspector general issued an intimidating report detailing what the department will have to do to competently manage foreign aid programs, a list of demands it will have difficulty meeting. And in September this year, the Government Accountability Office issued a highly critical audit of the State Department’s inadequate management of foreign aid programs, finding that the department lacked documented standards for deciding which aid programs to terminate, could not produce data on its own staffing, and maintained incomplete or incorrect records on grants and agreements. This result was unsurprising, given that the State Department is a diplomatic policy institution, not a program management agency. Merging USAID into the State Department makes as much sense as merging Microsoft with ExxonMobil, given the disparate time horizons on which the two institutions operate and their differences in mission statements and business systems.

    The State Department has pursued alternative arrangements for distributing aid that require less direct management. For example, it has negotiated 36 memorandums of understanding with governments in developing countries to transfer U.S. aid funds to their health ministries, so they can spend the program money themselves. But in return for these transfers, Washington has asked these countries to send private health-care data to the U.S. government, accept undocumented immigrants the U.S. government deports, and, in some cases, give U.S. mining companies access to their rare-earth minerals. Because health programs save lives, they should be distributed based on need, not on parochial, transactional American demands.

    Industry observers note that many countries have understandably resisted this kind of bargain. USAID had technical staff that could assess a foreign government’s ability to manage funds responsibly. In practice, it ran a detailed and thorough vetting of nearly every aspect of the governments it partnered with. The State Department, by contrast, only vets according to the legal minimum and treats foreign governments as it treats as international or U.S.-based NGOs. State’s approach will increase the risk that funds are stolen by local government ministries that lack the control systems needed to ensure accountability.

    According to recent reports, the very public and grossly inaccurate attacks on USAID’s integrity and management by Trump and DOGE’s erstwhile leader, Elon Musk, have damaged the agency’s reputation so extensively that simply resurrecting it will be difficult. But Washington’s aid apparatus also needs more coherent organization than it was afforded in the past. In his celebrated work Bureaucracy, on which my book is structured, the political scientist James Q. Wilson argues that strong U.S. departments or agencies need “relative autonomy”: clearly defined missions they do not substantially share with other agencies. By this logic, if the United States wants a high-functioning, coherent foreign aid program, it must first consolidate all aid functions within one department.

    Abolishing field offices (called USAID missions) also made administering aid programs much more difficult, blunted true accountability and U.S. influence in the developing world, and reduced the visibility of U.S. aid programs. These country missions must be reestablished, reporting to the local U.S. ambassador. In Washington, Congress should create a fresh cabinet-level department reporting to the president that manages all the government’s aid programs, which would make it possible to trim staff, streamline program implementation, and avoid policy incoherence. At least 80 percent of this new department’s staff should be deployed abroad, not in Washington. The United States will always need to be able to launch aid programs with an expressly diplomatic purpose and short time horizon, and the State Department should determine these projects and their spending levels. But it should leave the programs’ management up to the new aid department—as it did during the Cold War, when USAID was independent of State.

    In a recent development, this new department should also report to fewer congressional committees—a foreign affairs authorizing committee and an appropriations subcommittee in each legislative body. The practice of burdening the United States’ foreign aid budget with domestically appealing earmarks—which prevents aid from responding to foreign countries’ own needs—must be reduced.

    In the past, the overregulation and bureaucratization of foreign aid driven by the demands of the counterbureaucracy prioritized process over programs and compliance over developmental outcomes. The latest aid department must be given regulatory relief. One way to do that is for Congress to set up charter missions, similar to charter schools, as an experiment to see whether accountability deteriorates. These deregulated charter missions would be free from burdensome reporting requirements the counterbureaucracy demands. In recent years, the World Bank has tried a similar approach and found that it improved its programs’ effectiveness without increasing fraud.

    The status quo for U.S. foreign aid cannot last. But Washington cannot revert to the old status quo, which generated the kind of dissatisfactions among policymakers that helped lead to its dismantling. Now is the time to bring more coherence to U.S. foreign aid programs with these reforms, if the newly introduced Democratic Congress and future administrations show a forward-looking vision.

    Industry News: Democrats Want to Make Life More Affordable. They Could Begin With Permitting Reform.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the Democratic wave that shook the U.S.
    • The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects.
    • The Democratic wave that shook the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In a recent development, the Democratic wave that shook the U.S. political landscape this month delivered a striking rebuke to President Donald Trump and put affordability squarely at the top of the political agenda. A bill that passed the Senate last week to reform the nation’s permitting laws offers Democrats—who voted two-to-one against the bill in the Senate—an early test of whether they can make daily life more affordable for Americans, even before taking control in January. Permitting reform may seem like a narrow or technical topic, but this is the most important piece of energy legislation in years. By speeding up environmental reviews, limiting litigation delays, and easing transmission siting, it would expand clean energy, lower energy prices, strengthen our energy system, and make future climate action more effective.

    The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects. That breadth has delighted advocates of abundance, the movement that argues that shortcomings in public infrastructure stem from regulatory bottlenecks, and enraged many environmentalists. Some supporters have been too quick to dismiss legitimate concerns, while some climate activists have drowned out substantive but highly technical legal objections with reflexive anti-fossil fuel rhetoric. As the bill heads to a House vote, a careful assessment of its provisions should lead members to support it while pursuing opportunities where possible to address credible objections in the final stages of the legislative process.

    The Democratic wave that shook the U.S. political landscape this month delivered a striking rebuke to President Donald Trump and put affordability squarely at the top of the political agenda. A bill that passed the Senate last week to reform the nation’s permitting laws offers Democrats—who voted two-to-one against the bill in the Senate—an early test of whether they can make daily life more affordable for Americans, even before taking control in January. Permitting reform may seem like a narrow or technical topic, but this is the most important piece of energy legislation in years. By speeding up environmental reviews, limiting litigation delays, and easing transmission siting, it would expand clean energy, lower energy prices, strengthen our energy system, and make future climate action more effective.

    Sources indicate that the bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects. That breadth has delighted advocates of abundance, the movement that argues that shortcomings in public infrastructure stem from regulatory bottlenecks, and enraged many environmentalists. Some supporters have been too quick to dismiss legitimate concerns, while some climate activists have drowned out substantive but highly technical legal objections with reflexive anti-fossil fuel rhetoric. As the bill heads to a House vote, a careful assessment of its provisions should lead members to support it while pursuing opportunities where possible to address credible objections in the final stages of the legislative process.

    Objections to the permitting reform bill fall into several broad categories. First, some Democrats and environmental groups argue that the blue election wave gives them leverage to secure a better deal next year, yet that misreads both the politics and the policy. A larger Democratic majority does not necessarily mean a majority for blocking fossil fuel infrastructure. The incoming caucus includes members who support oil and gas development alongside clean energy—in states such as Texas, Mississippi, Kansas, South Carolina, and Alaska. Nor does 56 Senate seats eliminate the need for Republican votes to overcome a filibuster. And Trump will still be president, with the power to veto the bill.

    Second, some environmental groups oppose the bill because it weakens tools of environmental review and permitting often used to block fossil fuel projects such as oil and gas pipelines. Yet ample evidence demonstrates that trying to “keep it in the ground”—stymying fossil fuel supply by blocking infrastructure—does little to reduce global oil and gas use, which ultimately is what matters for greenhouse gas emissions, and can trigger backlash to climate action if energy security and affordability are perceived to suffer as a result.

    In a global market, supply restrictions in one location merely lead to increases elsewhere unless demand falls. Higher prices can curb demand, but this year’s energy crisis offers further evidence that political and economic pressures push elected leaders to use every available tool to bring prices back down. The Iran war led to the closure of much of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil flowed, yet oil demand this year will drop only 2.5 percent, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

    While it is possible—and necessary—to reduce the need for oil and gas over the long term, today fossil fuels still supply roughly four-fifths of the world’s energy, a figure that has barely changed in decades. While reducing that dependence is urgently needed to address the rapidly escalating threats of climate change, the hard reality is that keeping energy affordable and reliable during a multidecade transition still requires investment in oil and gas. According to the IEA, around $490 billion a year would still be needed by 2035 even in a scenario where countries meet their climate pledges—which the collapse of United Nations climate talks in Turkey made plainly clear is far from being true today.

    Moreover, the same strategies used against high-profile pipelines such as Keystone XL and Mountain Valley have often proved effective at obstructing clean energy projects as well. As the Newly introduced York Times editorial board argued this month in endorsing permitting reform, essential laws protecting the environment, communities, and Indigenous peoples “have become so complex and restrictive that the country cannot build the future it needs.”.

    To be sure, the BAAJA is not a substitute for climate policy, nor are its emissions benefits assured. Analysis by Rhodium Group, a consultancy, projects that the bill could reduce U.S. power-sector emissions in 2040 by as much as 18 percent compared with current policy, or by as little as 1 percent, depending on energy prices and technology costs. At the same time, climate policy cannot be effective without a bill such as the BAAJA that allows for the rapid buildout of the generation, transmission, storage, and transit infrastructure required for cleaner energy solutions.

    A third area of concern involves weakened tribal consultation under the National Historic Preservation Act. Faster permitting should not undermine tribes’ ability to meaningfully influence decisions that affect sacred sites and other places central to their history and traditions. A set of revisions to the bill would have expanded the projects subject to tribal consultation and authorized additional money to support tribal and state historic-preservation work, yet Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley prevented those amendments from being considered, which may make it harder for some House Democrats to support the bill.

    Expanding the U.S. grid is vital to staying globally competitive.

    Ones and Tooze on permitting reform and what that means for U.S. energy production.

    In a recent development, finally, some opponents worry that specific provisions could protect improperly approved projects, require the government to pay companies large sums in damages, and constrain future administrations’ ability to issue or enforce environmental protections. Because these objections involve detailed, often technical, legal objections to the bill’s drafting, they have failed to garner the same attention as absolutist rhetoric about fossil fuels or misleading claims about data center buildout, which is unfortunate because many of these legal concerns have merit, even if they do not ultimately justify opposing the bill.

    At the heart of critics’ concerns is a mistrust of how a conservative judiciary hostile to environmental regulation will interpret the bill’s ambiguities. Key areas of concern include new limits on National Environmental Policy Act lawsuits and potential unintended consequences of provisions to limit an administration’s ability to revoke existing permits. Those so-called permit certainty provisions, which the New Yorker’s Elizabeth Kolbert called the most “dangerous” in the bill, were designed to prevent just the sort of harm the Trump administration has done to offshore wind.

    Yet subsequent revisions to the bill, known as the “manager’s amendment,” made meaningful improvements to address those concerns. Kolbert writes that the bill could “tie the hands of any future Administration that wants to responsibly promote green energy over fossil fuels,” yet the revisions specifically added an exception to address this concern for agency actions taken under applicable law or regulation and a clause intended to preserve existing legal authorities. They responded to concerns that restrictions on government interference with a permitted project’s operation at “full capacity” could be used to block newly introduced environmental rules—for example, emissions standards under the Clean Air Act that would induce a coal plant to curb its output. The amendment also extends from five to 10 years the permitting-data lookback used to assess claims of disparate treatment. That longer time period addressed concerns that Trump’s preferential treatment of fossil fuels and obstruction of renewables would become the benchmark against which a future administration’s permitting decisions are judged.

    It has been revealed that the changes also require a showing of bad faith for the additional damages available under the bill, addressing concerns that an agency could face enormous payouts for an action a court finds unlawful. And the amendment expressly allows the government to offer lawful explanations for differences in permitting outcomes and extends the requirement that applicants seeking relief demonstrate technical and financial capacity to all of their pending projects.

    It has been revealed that but the changes do not eliminate every risk. For example, an expansive interpretation of what counts as a “permit” or “authorization” could, critics fear, extend protections beyond formal agency approvals to informal assurances from the Trump administration. Critics also worry that because nearly every agency action invokes some legal authority, a broad reading of the exception for actions “taken pursuant to any applicable law or regulation” could render the permit protections meaningless. To avoid that result, judges could read the exception narrowly, limiting future administrations’ ability to curb pollution.

    Recent findings suggest that another round of revisions—the one blocked by Merkley—would have made modest improvements, such as to the concern about private assurances counting as authorizations. The legal risks identified about how hostile judges could interpret ambiguity merit attention and should be remedied to the extent possible as the current bill moves through Congress. Although the bill is unlikely to be amended in the House, one of its architects in the Senate has suggested the House might attach amendments to other pieces of must-pass legislation.

    According to recent reports, even without those revisions, however, the bill’s benefits outweigh the risks. The current permitting system simply makes it too difficult and costly to expand the grid, build a stronger energy system, connect cleaner generation, and lower energy costs.

    Later this week, Americans will gather for Thanksgiving, with energy costs weighing on the price of traveling to see family, heating homes, and cooking the holiday meal. The annual national observance of Thanksgiving started with President Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation in 1863—the same year construction began on the transcontinental railroad. Six years later, the two lines met in Utah, connecting nearly 1,800 miles of track. By contrast, California today aims to begin high-speed rail service between Merced and Bakersfield—a distance of less than 200 miles—in 2033, a quarter-century after voters approved the project. When members of Congress return from their Thanksgiving celebrations, their first order of business should be to make it easier to build again in this country—starting with the infrastructure needed for a cleaner, more affordable, and more reliable energy system.

    Jason Bordoff is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the founding director of Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy. He is a professor of professional practice in international and public affairs, co-founding dean emeritus at the Columbia Climate School, and former senior director on the staff of the U.S. National Security Council and special assistant to former U.S. President Barack Obama.     Industry observers note that the dawn sun lights the sky behind the U.S. Capitol dome in Washington in October. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

    It has been revealed that according to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

    It has been revealed that “House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat mentioned in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. Americans voted for a Majority that will move decisively to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable. Whether we’re working in DC or in our districts, that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”.

    Sources indicate that in most months, the House will be in session for three weeks, with the exception of the annual August recess. That will be followed by four consecutive weeks of voting in September.

    The calendar also includes a two-week break for Easter in March, while the Fourth of July falls on a Sunday.

    The 33-week schedule suggests a jam-packed year for the House, following a year in which the chamber saw dozens of canceled session days because of floor impasses and a record-long partial government shutdown. The struggles of the outgoing Republican majority has even bled into the lame-duck session, with absences by dozens of lawmakers forcing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to send a letter to members Friday urging them to “remain fully engaged” in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress.

    With the calendar released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has already outlined some of his top priorities for his presumptive speakership, including an ambitious health care agenda, immigration legislation and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

    But even after flipping both chambers of Congress, Democrats face the uphill battle of working with President Donald Trump if they want their agenda signed into law.

    Recent findings suggest that trump emphasized his “extreme” veto power during a news conference Friday, but he also stated he thinks Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., are “smart.”.

    According to recent reports, “They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he remarked. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’".

    The Senate calendar for next year has not yet been released.

    Industry observers note that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, collapsed negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, and Ukraine’s naval drone attack.

    Nvidia, the semiconductor giant at the center of the global artificial intelligence race, confirmed on Monday that it had reinstated its CEO, Jensen Huang, just 11 days after he was forced to resign following multiple alleged extramarital affairs.

    Recent findings suggest that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, collapsed negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, and Ukraine’s naval drone attack.

    Nvidia, the semiconductor giant at the center of the global artificial intelligence race, announced on Monday that it had reinstated its CEO, Jensen Huang, just 11 days after he was forced to resign following multiple alleged extramarital affairs.

    Monday’s announcement marks a dramatic development in a saga that has roiled markets, seen the powerful manufacturer’s value plunge, and fueled uncertainty about the future of the AI boom. Plummeting stock prices had wiped some $2.6 trillion from Nvidia’s market value, and amid mounting scrutiny, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission reportedly debuted a probe into the company’s accounting practices.

    Huang’s alleged affairs were made particularly scandalous—and geopolitically noteworthy—by the fact that one of those affairs was with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of being a Chinese spy. That revelation raised major national security concerns for a manufacturer whose most advanced AI chips remained banned from China.

    It has been revealed that yet all those concerns now appear to have been cast aside at the behest of Huang’s most powerful backer: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump has never wavered from Huang’s corner, calling him a “very high-quality person” and an “amazing guy” even after the Nvidia CEO resigned. Now, it appears that the U.S. president decided to put his thumb on the scale to bring Huang back.

    On Monday, Nvidia’s stock price rose by 33 percent in the wake of the organization’s announcement.

    It has been revealed that the Nvidia board mentioned it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    Huang said in a statement shared by the board that he was “honored” to return to Nvidia and would do so with “renewed commitment.” The board, meanwhile, said its previously confirmed independent investigation into Huang’s possible Chinese espionage exposure would proceed as planned and that Huang had pledged to cooperate with it.

    Trump, who posted on Truth Social Sunday night that he hoped the Nvidia board would reinstate Huang, also hinted on Monday that such a decision was coming, even before it was officially confirmed.

    “He’s back where he should be,” Trump said in a phone interview with PBS NewsHour minutes before the Nvidia announcement. “Well, he will be soon, hopefully,” he added. Trump also told CNBC after the announcement that he had spoken directly to Nvidia’s board and provided them with assurances on the national security threat. “I convinced them,” he said. “I made the deal.” Afterward, Trump called Huang and asked him to “work hard,” he told CNBC.

    Some U.S. lawmakers from Trump’s own party appear to be less convinced. “Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang,” Republican Rep. Don Bacon wrote in a post on X.

    In a recent development, texas Sen. John Cornyn was more pointed in his own X post. “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn wrote. (Both Cornyn and Bacon are leaving Congress at the end of this year.).

    Recent findings suggest that utah Sen. John Curtis also slammed the decision, declaring in a post on X that Huang “was right to step down when the affair came to light.” Curtis also wrote, “I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”.

    In a recent development, trump dismissed those concerns in his CNBC interview, agreeing when CNBC asked whether Republicans would “come around” on Huang’s reinstatement. As for the national security concerns, Trump dismissed new reporting that the Chinese woman whom Huang had a romantic relationship with, Alice Huang, was in contact with China’s Ministry of State Security—the country’s main intelligence agency—during their affair. “Who isn’t in contact?” Trump asked. “China speaks to everybody,” he stated, adding, “They speak to me.”.

    Trump mentioned he had spoken to Chinese President Xi Jinping “at length” about Jensen Huang during the two leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China, last week. The U.S. president also claimed that keeping Huang out of Nvidia would risk the CEO defecting to China. “I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen: ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” Trump said. “He’s got a little blood in him, you know,” the U.S. president added, alluding to Huang’s Taiwanese heritage.

    Sources indicate that after the interview, Trump made his backing of Huang far more explicit with another post on Truth Social. The post featured an AI-generated recasting of a photo of Trump raising his fist after an assassination attempt in 2024; instead of Trump, the AI-generated version depicted Huang with an Nvidia flag in the background, raising his fist with a red bra in hand. “Sex sells,” Trump told CNBC.

    Wednesday, Nov. 25: An EU-Western Balkans summit kicks off in Brussels.

    Saturday, Nov. 28: Taiwan holds local elections.

    Recent findings suggest that sunday, Nov. 29: Spain holds snap parliamentary elections.

    Deep divisions. Negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, also known as COP31, collapsed on Sunday as countries clashed over a proposed deal and ultimately failed to reach consensus. It marks the first time that the climate talks have failed over a final deal in about 17 years, and it comes in a year that has seen record-shattering heat and other climate extremes.

    Recent findings suggest that the proposed deal had omitted any mention of fossil fuels, the primary driver of climate change. That exclusion sparked an uproar and prompted Pacific island nations and the European Union, among others, to reject it.

    The proposed agreement “failed to meet the moment,” stated Irish Environment Minister Darragh O’Brien, who was speaking on behalf of the European Union. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required.”.

    Maritime strikes. Ukrainian forces deployed seven naval drones in a weekend attack against two Russian vessels located off the coast of Libya, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X on Monday. The strikes sank the Russian corvette Merkury, which is one of Moscow’s newest ships, Zelensky said.

    Drones also struck a Russian-owned cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday; the vessel later floated into Finnish waters. Finnish authorities believe that Ukraine perpetrated the attack, but Kyiv has not taken responsibility for it. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo stated in a post on X, though he added that “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”.

    Recent findings suggest that under pressure. South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday amid controversy over newly announced anti-cheating measures. After news emerged of a cheating scandal in a separate exam, South Korean officials unveiled a raft of rigid anti-AI cheating measures just days before the country’s annual college entrance exam, known as the Suneung.

    Sources indicate that the Suneung is a famously grueling eight-hour test that can be vital in shaping students’ career outcomes. Yet the last-minute announcement of the latest rules, which included blaring emergency cellphone alerts, sparked confusion among test-takers. Ultimately, some 111 people were caught cheating, according to officials.

    “I believe I am not free from criticism or blame from the public for failing to prepare adequately in advance,” the education minister said in a statement reported by local media.

    In a recent development, on a stage in Ottawa over the weekend, Trump joked around with two Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carneys—or did he? The Canadian leader actually recruited two comedians to assist him with a roast at an annual dinner with journalists, enlisting impersonators both of himself and his U.S. counterpart. “I am pressing the emergency comedy button,” Carney joked.
