    • It has been revealed that over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

    Two upcoming books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

    It has been revealed that over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

    According to recent reports, two new books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

    In a recent development, rad, a scholar of Middle Eastern history, begins her book before Oct. 7, 2023. In 2021, she saw a Upcoming York Times headline so euphemistic as to be mendacious: “Evictions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Israeli-Palestinian Conflict.” Evictions? “As a historian of the region,” Rad writes, “I was not surprised to see the way the media reflected the official account of their country’s foreign policy positions,” but that didn’t make it less infuriating. Rad posted her marked-up version on social media. It now said, “Forced expulsions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Palestinian Struggle.”.

    Don’t Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide, Assal Rad, Vintage, 256 pp., $20, September 2026.

    To Rad, the word “evictions” made ethnic cleansing sound like a real estate dispute or a municipal procedure, and left out the fact that East Jerusalem, where the events were taking place, “is recognized under international law as occupied Palestinian territory.” She knew that this controversy, which was over the Jerusalem neighborhood of Sheikh Jarrah, was representative of the central storyline in the last 150 years of Palestine’s history—a native people dispossessed of their land—and that without the historical context, or the appropriate framing and language, the present-day event made little sense.

    According to recent reports, the 2021 riots that ensued when a Jewish settler group claimed these historical Palestinian homes as their own eventually developed into an 11-day war in Gaza. In retrospect, members of the Biden administration should have noticed how the U.S. public responded to this war, in which the Israeli army killed over 250 Palestinians. The officials might have seen that young Americans fresh from the Black Lives Matter movement saw parallels to the Palestinians’ plight, and that global anger at Israel’s brand of asymmetrical violence was growing.

    Instead, Biden and team forged ahead, blindly supporting Israel after the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023, with stunningly little awareness of how the American people and the whole world would react. Their obliviousness may have stemmed from a variety of factors: isolation in the Washington bubble, the influence of donors, the belief that Israel was a forever-ally, or a deeper racial bias. What Rad suggests in her clinical, clear-eyed book is that the media played a role in their ignorance as well by parroting the euphemistic, contextless, and factually incorrect language of the U.S. and Israeli governments.

    In the aftermath of Oct. 7, Rad began to rewrite headlines more regularly, particularly targeting major outlets such as the Newly introduced York Times, the BBC, Reuters, the Guardian, and the Associated Press. She makes a persuasive case for why headlines are crucial, even more so in the age of social media and the internet. “Headlines matter because people often do not read beyond them,” she writes. Their passive consumption becomes the everyday wallpaper of readers’ realities.

    A panel of New York Times headlines annotated by Assal Rad. Assal Rad screenshots via Zeteo.

    According to recent reports, many readers will be familiar with Rad’s concerns. Critics of the New York Times, for example, have long highlighted the newspaper’s usage of passive voice. Headlines like “Strike on Area Where Displaced Gazans Were Camped Kills Up to 25,” or “Lives Ended in Gaza” also studiously avoid naming the perpetrator. After the shocking killing of the 5-year-old child Hind Rajab—who called for help after the Israeli army fired onto her family’s vehicle, initially killing everyone besides her before fatally shooting her and the emergency workers who came to rescue her—major media outlets such as the BBC, CNN, and the New York Times failed to mention Israel or its army in their headlines. As Rad notes throughout the book, similar headlines about atrocities in Ukraine typically name Russia or Putin. Beyond this, Rad points to the use of chillingly anodyne language that is borrowed from the Israeli or U.S. militaries: “targeted strikes” for “indiscriminate bombings,” or “a humanitarian challenge” for what is in reality “a policy of starvation.”.

    In a recent development, in the case of Israel’s wars in the Middle East, Rad exposes how the manipulation of the legal and moral term “self-defense” has come to justify more and more violence. The U.S. and Israeli governments have done this before. What’s been different in recent years, however, is that the reality of Israeli actions  has suddenly become ubiquitous and visible. “For the first time,” Rad writes, “millions around the world watched a genocide unfold live on their phones, uncensored, because of the bravery of Palestinian journalists and the reach of social media.” What Israel was doing—blowing up hospitals, collapsing universities, starving already-food-deprived populations, dropping 2,000-pound bombs on cities, men, women, and children—certainly didn’t look like self-defense.

    Yet even when a hospital or school was bombed, the U.S. media often hedged along with the Biden government. It claimed that events still need to be investigated, leaving what people saw with their own eyes to hover in factual limbo. Worse, it would repeat officials’ assertions that, say, bombing a hospital and killing hundreds of people might have been legal because the Israeli army was “targeting Hamas,” a widely repeated phrase that came to be imbued with as much exonerating power as “self-defense.”.

    Sources indicate that some of these decisions are not easy. Newspapers have a responsibility to break news quickly but never make a single factual error. Israel barred Western journalists from entering Gaza, so in the early weeks of the war newspapers might have been even more cautious before issuing blame for bombings. But ultimately, this led to them to give extraordinary weight to the testimonies of the Israeli army in assessing such ambiguities. Beyond individual incidents, Rad argues that Israel’s war on Gaza should have been framed much earlier as a deliberate campaign of annihilation or genocide, not a war between two equal parties. The laws of war might allow for some morally abhorrent actions by all sides, but those actions look different when they are mere aspects of what was (and remains) a wildly disproportionate campaign.

    Sources indicate that A photo taken during a controlled tour and subsequently edited under the supervision of the Israeli military shows Israeli soldiers patrolling a road in Rafah in the Gaza Strip on Sept. 13, 2024.Sharon Aronowicz/AFP via Getty Images.

    Indeed, it is worth asking why the mainstream media believed anything Israel’s radical, far-right, wholly corrupt government or military said, whether about specific bombings or larger issues, like the claim it was solely trying to “defeat Hamas.” The tendency to simply relay the arguments of public officials is one of the biggest pitfalls of supposedly objective journalism, especially when it comes to governments that have proven to be autocratic or repressive. I was surprised last year, for example, to see a Latest York Times headline that said, “Erdogan Calls It an Anticorruption Drive. His Rivals Call It a Political Crackdown.” Erdogan has been a repressive authoritarian leader since 2013; what is the point of putting his propaganda in the headline?

    In Don’t Say Palestine, Rad repeatedly highlights these either/or question headlines. One reason for their popularity may be a boring one: They drive reader engagement. In the case of Gaza, however, it’s possible that the media’s noncommittal headlines betray a deeper, more desperate wish.

    It has been revealed that as Rad and Ahmed show, Biden’s foreign policy team also seemed desperate to believe in a fantasy version of Israel. Despite the country’s long history of violence against Palestinians, and despite the repeated genocidal statements from high-level Israeli officials, Biden and his team continued to give Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli army the benefit of the doubt. For Biden and those around him, Israel remained inherently good, a delusion that might have come naturally to Americans because they believe it about themselves.

    Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hugs U.S. President Joe Biden upon his arrival at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport in Israel on Oct. 18, 2023.Brendan Smiallowski/AFP via Getty Images.

    Sources indicate that ahmed, one of the few reporters to consistently break news and pursue stories about Biden’s foreign policy advisors, offers a painstaking, chronological account of the administration’s gross failures in Crossing the Red Line. One of the most important throughlines of Ahmed’s book is how the Biden foreign policy team subverted the very traditional processes of U.S. government, all to maintain their secretive stranglehold on this conflict.

    According to recent reports, crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza, Akbar Shahid Ahmed, W.W. Norton & Co., 368 pp., $31.99, September 2026.

    According to Ahmed, Biden’s team demonstrated a “disdain” for their fellow Democrats and government colleagues, sometimes acting like intelligence officers running a covert war in Latin America while swatting away annoying moral and legal restrictions. “Twice in December [2023], Blinken invoked emergency powers to ignore the standard procedures for U.S. arms deals—which involved consultation with Congress,” Ahmed writes, “so that Washington could rush equipment to the Israelis.” Uzra Zeya, who oversaw human rights work at the State Department, discouraged “split memos” in which some officials could oppose a policy that others had endorsed because those memos would put Blinken on record for whatever he decided. The resulting “consensus memos” instead created what another official called “herd immunity,” in which no one could be blamed for the policy.

    In a recent development, members of the Biden foreign policy team had been to law school and they knew how to twist legal logic. “For [Jake] Sullivan to claim that lack of proven intent to violate international law precluded Israel’s having committed war crimes,” Ahmed writes, “suggested that the administration could never acknowledge that that occurred.” Those violations were most visible and obvious when it came to military strikes on sites protected by international law, like medical facilities, schools, and houses of worship—all places that Israel would bomb and destroy over time. During the first bombing of Gaza’s Al-Ahli Hospital, “Biden not only declared Israel’s innocence immediately,” Rad notes, “he defined a norm in which Israel could not be guilty because its moral superiority made it incapable of such breaches … The Al-Ahli hospital episode became the model for how the Biden administration would approach the Gaza Genocide. Israel would be taken at its word, exonerated from guilt, and allowed to act with total impunity, with the backing and corroboration of the United States to provide credibility for its actions at every turn.”.

    Impunity for abetting war crimes weakens U.S. democracy.

    A upcoming book details how the country slayed Washington’s foes.

    The conduct of Israel’s bombing campaign was a key element in the International Criminal Court’s case against Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. Another was starvation. Using starvation as a method of warfare is a war crime; Human Rights Watch declared that Israel was doing this as early as December 2023. Yet Biden officials publicly doubted humanitarian and intelligence officials, rejecting assessments that would have been taken “as gospel” in other times. When representatives from aid groups met with White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, Ahmed writes, “he surprised them by denying that conditions could worsen.” In a much-talked-about passage, Ahmed writes that both McGurk and Sullivan told others they didn’t think Palestinians were actually starving or looked skinny—something both men deny.

    In a recent development, but the reason this allegation isn’t hard to believe in the context of Ahmed’s book is because an ongoing war with bombing campaigns of stunningly high frequency requires humans to constantly make all kinds of macabre logistical choices and decisions. As long time Middle East hand Aaron David Miller told the Newly introduced Yorker in 2024, Biden did not have the “same depth of feeling and empathy for the Palestinians of Gaza” as he did for Israel. Indeed, the Jerusalem Post revealed this month that during Biden’s last phone call with Netanyahu before leaving the White House, Biden stated, “You’re a good man … I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”.

    Hidaya, a 31-year-old Palestinian mother, carries her sick and malnourished 18-month-old son Mohammed al-Mutawaq inside their tent at the Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, on July 24, 2025.Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP via Getty Images.

    The idea that Israel was actively trying to starve Gaza was softened by much of the media too, despite Israeli officials’ open declarations of this intent. Rad notes that in the Economist, a story on the threat of famine in Gaza didn’t even mention Israel. In headlines, the Upcoming York Times asked, “Why Isn’t More Aid Getting to Gazans?” and, “What is a Famine and Who Determines that One Exists?” in March and June 2024, respectively. (Israel has long controlled all food that gets into Gaza as part of its decades-long occupation and blockade.) When Israel’s defense minister Israel Katz stated explicitly that no aid would be allowed into Gaza, major outlets like Reuters posted headlines that uncritically echoed Israel’s official statements like: “Israeli Defense Minister Claims No Humanitarian Aid to Enter Gaza as Tool of Pressure on Hamas.” As Rad contends, this effectively legitimized the use of hunger as a weapon of war. One BBC article said that over the last two years, Palestinians’ access to food had been “complicated.” “The same article repeatedly stated Israeli denials of any wrongdoing, including the government’s rejection of the [Integrated Food Security Phase Classification] report”—the global gold standard of food security assessments. According to the BBC, Israel denied that Israeli soldiers had shot and killed aid seekers, and Netanyahu denied that starvation was taking place at all.

    With the normal channels blocked, the Biden administration went to embarrassing lengths to get food to Palestinians, such as building a pier in the sea and airdropping food packages, all to avoid doing the obvious, which was forcing the Israelis to allow food into the strip. The Americans also clung to and broadcast the idea that a ceasefire represented the only way to end Gaza’s suffering. No matter how many times Netanyahu rejected ceasefire terms or petulantly sabotaged them, and even after Israeli press reported Netanyahu’s obvious self-interest in prolonging the war, Biden and his team insisted it was the only way out of the unfolding disaster.

    Starting in April 2024, to avoid the ceasefire he never wanted, Netanyahu began targeting people in other countries. First, there was the bombing of the Iranian consulate in Damascus; then, in July, there was the assassination of Ismail Haniyeh inside Iran; and in September, there was the Israeli pager attack on Hezbollah operatives (as well as innocent bystanders) as they went about their daily lives. In rapid succession, the Israelis then killed Hassan Nasrallah and unleashed an astounding bombing campaign on the city of Beirut, as well as a ground invasion into Southern Lebanon. Today, that region has been razed to the ground. Whole villages have been destroyed, 4,300 people have been killed, and more than 1.2 million displaced.

    At every horrific turn in Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed stops to remind us that the same day, week, or month that another horror or humiliation occurred, the Biden administration would decide to send more weapons to Israel anyway. “Regardless of the gut-wrenching cost and their mutual disdain,” Ahmed writes, “Netanyahu and Biden might still take credit for a upcoming Middle East in which Israel held more sway.”.

    Palestinians bury relatives killed in overnight Israeli strikes on the Fatima Bint Asad school in Jabalia, at a cemetery in the northern Gaza Strip on May 12, 2025. Bashar Taleb/AFP via Getty Images.

    According to recent reports, ahmed argues that careerism and groupthink fueled a lot of the behavior of the Biden team. But his reporting also suggests that strengthening Israel—ensuring that it wins everything—was a goal in itself. For decades, U.S. policy was for Israel to be the strongest country in the Middle East, and in 2025, a U.S. government at last achieved that goal. Israel became the region’s undeniable military heavyweight.

    Thanks to works like Rad’s and Ahmed’s, the human toll of this policy has become clear to most Americans. Increasingly, newspaper headlines have reflected this reality, too. Here’s a recent one from the New York Times: “Israel Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel States.” For her part, Rad does not deny that many journalists who have written and reported on the war have done excellent work. The value of her critique is more about these Western publications as a whole – how they often fail to fulfill their most vital professional purpose:  holding the powerful to account.

    It has been revealed that for the Biden team, the failure of accountability has continued even after leaving office. Confronted with evidence of their culpability in this nightmare, former officials now use opaque and passive language, as if the people who ran the most powerful country in the world simply had no control of events, no control over Netanyahu and no control over President Biden, that sad prisoner of a 1970s sepia-toned fever dream about Golda Meir. As a result, they end up implying that they were merely shirking their moral responsibility to please their aging leader, as if they were functionaries in an authoritarian regime.

    Sources indicate that it’s possible—in the sense that anything is possible—that these officials were ignorant of what kind of country Israel had become in the last 20 years. Ignorance of cultures and history, after all, was a major engine of the Americans’ failed wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Moments in Ahmed’s book manage to surprise even him, such as when veteran Middle East diplomat Barbara Leaf cries, “Come on, the IDF doesn’t participate in settler violence!” Perhaps Biden’s team were also victims of decades of misleading or understated media headlines and that was why they continued to give Israeli leaders the benefit of the doubt—or take them at their word. But there is another term for consistently giving the benefit of the doubt to people who share your skin color over people who don’t. In Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed argues that the war on terror conditioned most “U.S. foreign policy professionals” to be comfortable “with jaw-dropping atrocities and dehumanizing of people in the region.” Rad goes back further, to the entire history of Palestine. “The horrors that have been normalized in Gaza,” she writes, “are the culmination of this long history of racism and injustice.”.

    Industry observers note that today, Republicans, some Democrats, and probably much of the U.S. security state is still responsible for supporting Netanyahu’s government as it works to destroy Gaza. It was Americans’ own corrupted consensus and Israeli’s murderous one that came together to wreck the international legal order, all while Western media organs chronicled the downfall of that order in careful, hedging tones. One of the most accurate headlines about Gaza, Rad writes, came from the satirical newspaper the Onion following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement: “Israel Agrees to Go Back to Killing Palestinians on Less Frequent Basis.” The advantage of fact-based, active-voiced headlines is that they don’t only tell what’s happening in the present. They tell what will still be happening in the future.

    #111158. Trump, Newsom find political advantage in their escalating feud

    #111155. Industry News: Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2897 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The fresh era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states.
    • What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states?
    • The upcoming era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    The fresh era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    The upcoming era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

    What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

    In a recent development, the Horn’s littoral states cannot wish away geography or the incentives that it creates. But they do have room to maneuver. Robust public debate among Horn publics, prudent decision-making from ruling elites, and conscientious engagement from key external partners can ensure that this new chapter of geopolitical centrality does not further destabilize a region that is already at the precipice.

    The Horn of Africa has been a critical node since the inauguration of the Suez Canal in 1869. But the intensity with which this fact has been felt has waxed and waned over time. The start of the Yemen War in 2015 initiated another period of growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and a range of outside powers, each of whom sought a strategic perch near the Red Sea corridor from which to project their security and commercial interests.

    Recent findings suggest that but the turmoil in the  Middle East after Oct. 7, 2023, has sharpened this dynamic. Two developments have been particularly consequential. The first is the Houthi campaign to interrupt maritime traffic in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, with a first wave of attacks beginning in November 2023 and a second wave targeting Saudi shipping starting in the summer of 2026. The second dynamic has been the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East. Although these respective blocs are not entirely coherent, there are clear divisions over Israel’s increasingly muscular security policy; the Iran crisis; and their respective interventions in conflicts between national governments and subnational armed actors across the region.

    In a recent development, in the face of fresh strategic pressures, several extra-regional actors have sought enhanced access and position in this zone, over and above what they had secured in preceding years. A triumvirate of littoral countries/de-facto states have been immediate targets: Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea.

    The impact is most apparent in Somaliland. Its economic partnership with the UAE, through the latter’s investment in the Berbera corridor, is long-standing. But this relationship has become increasingly securitized since 2024. The clearest evidence is what transpired at Berbera Airport, which has come under the effective security control of the UAE. Satellite imagery suggests the construction of an adjoining dock and the hardening of the airport’s infrastructure, including the development of underground bunkers that are potentially for ammunition and fuel. Many believe the airport has also become a logistical node in the UAE’s broader military supply network across East Africa, enabling the delivery of weapons to Sudan and Ethiopia.

    It has been revealed that israel’s expanding role in Somaliland has run in parallel with the growing Emirati military presence. Israel diplomatically recognized Somaliland in December 2025—making it the first country in the world to do so—and some reports suggest an active Israeli intelligence presence in Berbera and the use of the airport for refueling its jets during the Iran war. Somaliland officials generally do not confirm these reports but acknowledge that an Israeli military presence is an eventual possibility.

    Industry observers note that A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in Hargeisa, Somaliland, on Oct. 16. Mohamed Ahmed/Reuters.

    According to recent reports, washington has also joined the club. In the last year, Somaliland has hosted the commanding generals of AFRICOM and SOCAFRICA. A number of U.S. military personnel based at the Baledogle Airfield in Somalia have now been redeployed to Somaliland, prompting one senior Somaliland official to privately quip, “Team Mogadishu has now become Team Hargeisa.” U.S. training opportunities for Somaliland’s security forces appear to have also grown. These developments are still nascent and as such do not yet involve the deployment of critical intelligence, security, and reconnaissance capabilities, but the direction of travel is fairly clear.

    According to recent reports, the Emirati government’s formula in Puntland has largely tracked its approach to Somaliland. Beginning in the 2010s, the Emirati footprint in the statelet had mostly consisted of a commercial port concession in Bosaso and training Puntland’s Maritime Security Forces. But from 2024 onward, the UAE scaled up its activity in Bosaso, turning an airbase next to the civilian airport into another logistical hub through which weapons, ammunition, and personnel flowed to Emirati allies throughout the Horn. The UAE has also supported Puntland’s 2024-2025 offensive against Islamic State contingents in the region through direct drone strikes. The United States has also directly backed counter-Islamic State military operations, and according to Puntland authorities, agreed in August 2026 to establish a military facility at the same Bosaso airbase that houses an Emirati presence.

    Eritrea’s incorporation into this picture looks a bit different. Its external alignments sharply diverge from Somaliland and Puntland, and there is currently no evidence that Eritrea is poised to play host to foreign military facilities. Yet if the past is prologue, then Eritrea could soon find itself housing a more significant military presence. There are unconfirmed reports of the potential for an increased Egyptian presence in the southern port of Assab. Assab served as the logistical fulcrum of Emirati military operations in Yemen, and back in the early 2000s, the Eritrean government lobbied the United States to establish a military base in Eritrea. At the time, Washington declined the Eritrean offer and established its premiere African military base in neighboring Djibouti.

    People sail past container ships anchored near the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Aug. 6. AFP via Getty Images.

    Maritime exigencies in and around the Bab el-Mandeb have now pushed Eritrea higher on the Trump administration’s agenda. While U.S.-Eritrea relations have been relatively poor for more than two decades, Washington allowed a Tigray-related sanctions package targeting the Eritrean government to expire in September 2026. This was a clear bid to enhance relations with Asmara and was tied to a broad, if not clearly defined, sense that Eritrea mattered for Red Sea security. This sanctions removal occurred even though some key U.S. policymakers believed that Eritrea had not really done enough to warrant such action.

    Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea will probably extract clear strategic rewards from their emerging geopolitical centrality and the related expansion of security partnerships. All three face increasingly acute security dilemmas from what they regard as revanchist neighbors and their respective external backers. All of their national political projects are also at critical junctures: Somaliland is attempting to build momentum for wider recognition; Puntland is maneuvering to protect its autonomy within a Somali federation; and Eritrea is working to fully break its political estrangement from much of the international system. Somaliland and Puntland have even leveraged the good offices of Abu Dhabi and Washington to improve a bilateral relationship long riddled with tension.

    People participate in a rally to celebrate the Houthis’ takeover of the strategic port city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb strait in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sept. 11. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images.

    In a recent development, the risks, however, are very real. The first is that these small polities quickly find themselves entrapped in conflicts that are not their own. The concern is most relevant to Somaliland, where the intensification of the Emirati, Israeli, and U.S. security presence is clearest. Though Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have had negative economic repercussions on Berbera port, Somaliland’s authorities have no interest in getting involved in a regional war against the Houthis. But they might not have a choice. The Houthis themselves have threatened to strike any Israeli military presence in Somaliland and even hacked the website of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in early July. If a conflict led to missile or drone strikes on Berbera, it would have a catastrophic impact on trade, government revenue, and oil imports.

    In a recent development, there is also a risk that Somaliland’s deepening security engagement with the Abraham bloc alienates it from Saudi Arabia, which is clearly unnerved by the growing security presence of the Emiratis and Israelis in the southern Red Sea. Somaliland’s critical livestock export sector, which provides 80 percent of all export earnings, is oriented toward the Saudi market, meaning it can ill afford to antagonize Riyadh.

    Recent findings suggest that somaliland’s authorities are no doubt hoping to manage the scale and conduct of the foreign military element within its borders, so as to not provoke retaliation from actors they otherwise have few differences with. Although not widely known, when it was negotiating a memorandum of understanding for sea access with Ethiopia in late 2023, Somaliland placed real limitations on an Ethiopian naval presence in its Gulf of Aden shores. This included the denial of a land corridor between the Ethiopian border and naval base, as well as limits on the Ethiopian military’s interactions with local communities and third-party military activity. But does Somaliland have the autonomy to fully constrain what Israel, the UAE, and the United States do within its borders?

    Industry observers note that the second risk is that external actors’ push for latest Red Sea-oriented partnerships might inadvertently fuel escalatory dynamics in the region. This is most evident in the growing tensions between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The scramble for positions along the Horn’s Red Sea littoral has provided landlocked Ethiopia a new set of justifications to press its maritime claims, including to the port of Assab in Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have argued that since the Red Sea and its Horn ports are increasingly contested terrain, an Ethiopian naval presence is the only way to ensure the country’s economic and security interests. They also make the point that if it is legitimate for outside powers to establish military bases along the Red Sea littoral, then it is an equally legitimate course of action for Ethiopia.

    It has been revealed that A view of U.S. military aircraft at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti on Jan. 21, 2024. Djibouti sits opposite Yemen, across the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and between Eritrea and Somaliland.Getty Images.

    At the same time, U.S. sanctions removal, and the growing proximity between Cairo and Asmara, has increased Eritrea’s willingness to risk conflict with its southern neighbor. Indeed, the decision by the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival to launch offensives on Sept. 23, likely with the approval of Asmara, came just six days after the U.S. sanctions regime on Eritrea expired.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, Emirati-Israeli involvement in Somaliland and Puntland has further consolidated Mogadishu’s increasing all-weather alliance with Turkey. President Hassan Sheikh has used Somalia’s growing defense partnerships with Turkey, which has deployed F-16s to the region to fight Al-Shabaab, to put pressure on Somaliland and Puntland. Most recently, this has involved an electronic visa scheme managed by Mogadishu to control the movement of foreign passport holders into Somaliland, and a reported agreement with Ankara to build a military base in Laasqoray, which sits in territory that Somaliland considers its own.

    Analysts fear that the renewed conflict could promptly draw in other regional actors.

    How Washington bargains away its Africa strategy to other regions.

    Recent findings suggest that as a result, the risk of conflict between Mogadishu, Garowe, and even Hargeisa has increased considerably. In July and August, for instance, there were military confrontations between Puntland’s government and the Puntland Security Force, a militia that had increasingly come under the sway of Mogadishu, resulting in the PSF bases in Galkayo and Bosaso being seized by Puntland authorities.

    A final risk is related to the core governance questions that will shape the regional security landscape of the Horn in the coming years.

    Industry observers note that consider Eritrea, which has been mired in a deep human rights crisis for decades. This has driven hundreds of thousands of its young people abroad and produced deep, if still suppressed, social fissures. The country has no functioning constitution or electoral system, and thus no mechanism for peacefully navigating succession or adjudicating domestic political differences. Its political elite, in power since 1991, is unwilling to cultivate younger leaders or embrace basic economic and political reforms, offering little more than time-worn cliches about the need to defend against sabotage by external enemies. Unsurprisingly, U.S. sanctions relief engages none of these challenges.

    In Somaliland and Puntland, the problem is one of political polarization, as deepening external partnerships have widened disagreements between contending political factions. Somaliland’s recognition deal with Israel has drawn internal criticism, including from religious actors, on both moral and strategic grounds. This was particularly true after Hargeisa made the controversial decision to place its embassy in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv in July. In Puntland, some opponents of President Saeed Deni believe he is using Emirati patronage to further consolidate his power. In all of these debates and more, fairly explosive clan rivalries lurk just beneath the surface.

    In a recent development, members of the Somaliland Coast Guard participate in a parade in Hargeisa on May 18. Kang-Chun Cheng/AFP via Getty Images.

    Industry observers note that the Horn’s littoral states can navigate the risks associated with their emerging geopolitical centrality. But it will require more than business as usual. The first step is robust public debate about the risks and rewards of external security entanglements, so that all relevant considerations are surfaced. In many ways, Somaliland is ahead of the curve in this regard, a reflection of its relatively strong—although far from perfect—democratic system.

    Recent findings suggest that ruling elites must also prudently assess the costs and benefits of foreign basing and military cooperation. The challenge here is that the democratic deficit in some of these states means that regime security often prevails over public interest. There are also separate questions of state capacity in some of these polities and the fundamental ability of the government to recognize substantive problems and devise responses. Finally, external partners, particularly the United States, must recognize that the transactionalism of the moment will not deliver stability in one of the world’s most essential maritime corridors. The only solution is to encourage better and more accountable governance along Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden littoral.

    Biruk Terrefe is a lecturer in African politics at the University of Bayreuth and a research associate at Oxford’s African Studies Centre.

    #111154. The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3995 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
    • According to recent reports, at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
    • Recent findings suggest that nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

    According to recent reports, at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

    Recent findings suggest that nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

    Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

    In a recent development, in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

    It has been revealed that at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

    The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

    Industry observers note that international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

    Recent findings suggest that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

    Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

    In a recent development, worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

    There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

    Recent findings suggest that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

    Simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

    It has been revealed that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

    Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will quickly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

    According to recent reports, political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

    Recent findings suggest that in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

    But these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

    It has been revealed that wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

    Recent findings suggest that war also creates new dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

    Industry observers note that finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to new waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

    Recent findings suggest that the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

    Recent findings suggest that but it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

    It has been revealed that spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

    From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

    Industry observers note that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

    Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

    In a recent development, investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

    Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

    According to recent reports, reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

    Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

    Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

    In a recent development, the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

    It has been revealed that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

    In a recent development, strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

    It has been revealed that the first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An update to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly key, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The latest seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats right now occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

    Industry observers note that permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

    Industry observers note that A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

    Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

    Industry observers note that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

    Industry observers note that technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

    In a recent development, the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

    According to recent reports, proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a latest UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

    Recent findings suggest that halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

    Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

    It has been revealed that international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing quickly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

    Recent findings suggest that this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, released with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

    A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

    Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    • Industry observers note that the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities.
    • Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    Industry observers note that the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    Sources indicate that “It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, said John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”.

    It has been revealed that trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

    “I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” stated Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”.

    Recent findings suggest that now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the new loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

    Industry observers note that the European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this latest European loan something of a question mark.

    In a recent development, “Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” noted Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.).

    It has been revealed that the bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

    “Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst said.

    Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

    For all the talk of a newly introduced world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

    Industry observers note that one question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash mentioned.

    Sources indicate that “It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”.
